intro.t: The church begins, and the gospel goes out.
b: Acts tells how the message of Jesus spread from a handful of followers in Jerusalem to the capital of the Roman world in about thirty years. Jesus’ words in 1:8 give the outline: ‘you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem (chapters 1–7), and in all Judea and Samaria (8–12), and to the ends of the earth (13–28).’ The first half centres on Peter, the second on Paul.

The real main character is the Holy Spirit, who empowers, guides and sends. Acts is full of real places and real officials, many confirmed by archaeology (see the drop-downs), and full of ordinary people, men and women, Jews and Gentiles, brought into one church.

Acts is the second volume of a two-part work; the ‘first book’ (1:1) is Luke’s Gospel, and both are addressed to Theophilus. From the 2nd century the church named the author as Luke, the doctor and travelling companion of Paul (Colossians 4:14; Philemon 24; 2 Timothy 4:11). Many scholars accept this, though some think the author was a later member of Paul’s circle. Three passages switch from ‘they’ to ‘we’ (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16), quietly showing that the writer was present for those journeys.

Date. Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome for two years, probably about AD 60–62, without saying how his trial ended. Some scholars, such as F. F. Bruce, think this suggests it was written in the early 60s, before Nero’s persecution of AD 64 and Paul’s death. Many others date it to AD 70–90, after Luke’s Gospel, which they date after AD 70. Either way, the writer was close to the events.

b: Where scholars stand. Some critical scholars, such as Ernst Haenchen, have regarded Acts mainly as theology in story form, written to present Paul and the church in a good light, with history shaped to fit. Others, including many classical historians, regard it as a careful work of ancient history. The debate continues.

The case for Luke as a careful historian. F. F. Bruce summed it up: Luke’s pages are full of city magistrates, provincial governors and client kings, and these references ‘time after time prove to be just right for the place and time in question’. Examples, with drop-downs at the passages: the ‘politarchs’ of Thessalonica (17:6), a title once thought to be Luke’s mistake and now found on dozens of inscriptions; Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, fixed by an inscription at Delphi (18:12); the Asiarchs and the town clerk of Ephesus (19:31, 35); the ‘chief man’ of Malta (28:7); and the death of Herod Agrippa I, told independently by Josephus (12:20). His account of the voyage and shipwreck in chapter 27 is still one of the most important sources on ancient seamanship.

Real difficulties. Luke selects and shapes his material, and the speeches are summaries in his own words, as was normal in ancient history. A few points are hard to fit with other sources, such as the date of Theudas (5:36, see the drop-down). Honest readers note these, and also note how often Luke has been vindicated where he was once doubted.

1.h: The question they ask, and the one he answers
1.t: They want to know about the restoration of the kingdom to Israel. Jesus does not correct the hope, he reframes its scope: not a date to be calculated but a mission to be carried out, and verse 8 is the table of contents for the whole book — Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, the ends of the earth.

The ascension is not Jesus disappearing but Jesus being enthroned. The promise that he will return in the same way makes the second coming bodily and visible, which rules out spiritualised readings of it.

1.h: Casting lots, for the last time
1.t: The replacement of Judas restores the Twelve to their symbolic completeness before Pentecost. Note that this is the final time in Scripture anyone seeks guidance by lot; after chapter 2 the Spirit is given, and the method never recurs.

2.t: Fifty days after Passover, at the feast celebrating the giving of the law at Sinai. Wind and fire are both Sinai imagery. What was written on stone is now written on people, exactly as Jeremiah 31 promised.
At Babel one language became many and the people scattered. Here many languages hear one message and people are gathered. Luke lists the nations deliberately.

Peter's argument is almost entirely Old Testament: Joel, Psalm 16, Psalm 110. He does not ask them to accept a new religion but to recognise that their own Scriptures have been fulfilled. The conclusion in verse 36 — God has made him both Lord and Christ — is the point everything builds to.

Peter ties baptism and forgiveness together in one sentence, which has been read in two ways: that baptism conveys forgiveness, or that it is the appointed sign of the repentance and faith through which forgiveness comes. The second is the Reformed and broadly evangelical reading, and the rest of Acts supports it — in chapter 10 the Spirit falls before anyone is baptised. However you read the order, the New Testament never imagines an unbaptised Christian. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.
Four things: the apostles' teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, prayer. Everything the church has since become complicated about is in that one verse in its simplest form.

3.h: Silver and gold I do not have
3.t: The healing happens at the temple gate, to a man who had been carried there daily for years. Note that Peter takes him by the hand — the same physical directness Jesus used.
Peter grants that they did not know what they were doing, which is startling given what they did. The offer of repentance is extended to the men who called for the crucifixion weeks earlier.

4.t: The exclusivity claim of the New Testament, stated plainly by a fisherman to the ruling council. It is worth noticing that this is said in a courtroom, under threat, rather than in a sermon to sympathetic hearers.
The council's assessment is accurate and their explanation is the key: they recognised that these men had been with Jesus. Competence is not what is being described.

5.t: The severity troubles people, and it should. The sin is not withholding — Peter says the property and the money were theirs — but lying to appear more generous than they were. It happens at the foundation of the church, and the effect is fear, which Luke reports without apology. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

5.h: Why did Ananias and Sapphira die
5.t: Their sin was not keeping money back — Peter says it was theirs — but lying to God to appear more generous than they were, at the very foundation of the church. Luke records the fear it produced without softening it. The episode is exceptional rather than a pattern: the New Testament does not expect such judgement to follow every sin, and later passages show great patience with serious failure. It stands as a warning that God is not mocked, especially where religion becomes performance. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

5.h: Lied to the Spirit, lied to God
5.t: Peter names the Holy Spirit as the one lied to, then in the next breath names God. The two statements are doing the same work, which is one of the clearest indications in Acts of the Spirit's full deity.

Sound counsel from a man who is not a believer, and Luke records it because history vindicated it. It is not, however, a reliable general principle: plenty of false movements have outlasted a generation.

6.t: A complaint about unequal treatment of Greek-speaking widows. Note the solution: the apostles do not take it on themselves but delegate, and all seven men chosen have Greek names — the complaining group is given the responsibility.

7.t: The longest speech in Acts, and it is a retelling of Israel's history with one thread pulled through it: God has always worked outside the land and outside the temple, and his people have always resisted those he sent.
Stephen sees Jesus standing — not seated — at God's right hand, and prays directly to him. His final words echo Jesus' own on the cross. Watching it is a man named Saul.

8.t: The scattering that was meant to destroy the church spreads it. Luke notes drily that those scattered preached wherever they went, and the gospel reaches Samaria as verse 1:8 said it would.

Reading Isaiah 53 and asking who the prophet means. Philip begins from that passage and tells him about Jesus, which is a model for how the Old Testament is to be preached. The man goes back to Africa with the message.

9.t: The question Jesus asks — why do you persecute me — identifies himself with the church he is not physically among. Paul's conversion is not a decision he arrives at but an intervention he is subjected to, which shapes everything he later writes about grace.
Nobody trusted Saul, understandably. Barnabas vouched for him, and the entire Gentile mission traces back through that one act of risk.

10.h: Cornelius, and the conversion of Peter
10.t: This chapter is usually called the conversion of Cornelius, but the man who changes most is Peter. The vision is repeated three times because he resists it twice.
The theological breakthrough of the book. Peter's summary of the gospel here is the shortest in Acts and worth memorising.

11.t: The first church where Gentiles are evangelised as a matter of course, and the place believers are first called Christians — probably as a nickname by outsiders. It becomes the base for everything that follows.

12.h: Praying for something and not believing it
12.t: The church prays for Peter's release, and when he turns up at the door they tell the servant girl she is out of her mind. Luke's sense of humour is real and this is the clearest example of it.

13.t: The Holy Spirit speaks in the first person — set apart for me — and claims both the calling and the men. Forces do not speak that way.
Paul's first recorded sermon already contains the doctrine of justification by faith, and states it as something the law of Moses could not accomplish.

14.t: The same crowd that tried to sacrifice to them drags Paul out for dead within days. Paul's speech to pagans here is entirely different from his synagogue preaching — he starts from creation rather than from Scripture.
Having just been stoned, Paul goes back to the cities he was driven from to strengthen the disciples, telling them hardship is the road in. He is not offering an easy gospel.

15.t: The most consequential meeting in church history. The question is whether Gentile converts must become Jews first, and the answer is no — salvation is by grace through faith for everybody on the same terms.

15.h: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us
15.t: The council names the Spirit alongside themselves as party to the decision, which is not how anyone speaks about an impersonal influence.
Over John Mark, who had abandoned them earlier. Luke reports the sharp disagreement without resolving it. Mark later becomes useful to Paul and writes a Gospel.

16.t: The Spirit prevents them twice before the Macedonian vision. Guidance in Acts is as often a blocked route as a clear call.
Luke's description of Lydia's conversion puts the initiative squarely with God. She is already a worshipper, already listening — and still the opening is done to her.
Singing after a beating, an earthquake, and a jailer who was about to kill himself. The question he asks and the answer he gets are about as compressed as the gospel gets.

17.t: Commended for checking the Scriptures daily to see whether what Paul said was true — of an apostle. The public-domain Bible on this site takes its name from them.
Paul quotes pagan poets rather than Scripture, starts from an altar they built themselves, and still ends at repentance and resurrection. Contextualisation without dilution.

18.t: Paul evidently needed telling. He stays in Corinth eighteen months, which is the longest he has settled anywhere so far.

19.t: The Ephesian converts destroy magic scrolls worth fifty thousand drachmas — roughly fifty thousand days' wages. Repentance costs them something specific.
The silversmiths' objection is commercial and only afterwards religious. Luke lets Demetrius say so himself.

20.h: Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders
20.t: The only speech in Acts addressed to Christian leaders. Note verse 28: the church of God, bought with his own blood — one of the strongest statements of Christ's deity in the book, and a disputed text worth knowing about.

20.h: A saying not in the Gospels
20.t: More blessed to give than to receive is attributed to Jesus but appears in none of the four Gospels. Evidence that more of his teaching circulated than was written down.

21.t: Agabus predicts Paul's imprisonment accurately; the believers conclude he should not go. Paul disagrees. The prediction is from the Spirit; the inference drawn from it is not.

22.t: Paul's testimony, adapted for a Jewish crowd in Aramaic. Luke gives the Damascus road three times in this book. The detail that ends the speech — sent to the Gentiles — is what ends the hearing.

23.t: Paul sets Pharisee against Sadducee on the resurrection. Shrewd, arguably too shrewd, and Luke neither praises nor criticises it.

24.t: Paul speaks about righteousness, self-control and the judgement to come, and Felix is frightened enough to send him away — then keeps him two years hoping for a bribe. The most honest picture in Scripture of a man who is interested but will not move.

25.t: A Roman citizen's right, and the mechanism by which Paul gets to Rome at imperial expense. God's purposes run through legal procedure here rather than around it.

26.t: Agrippa's reply is famously ambiguous in the Greek and may be sarcasm. Paul's answer — that he wishes everyone listening were as he is, except for the chains — is one of the warmest things he ever said.

27.t: An unusually detailed sea narrative, and one of the passages where Luke's eyewitness accuracy can be checked against what is known of ancient seafaring. It holds up.

28.t: Paul closes his ministry in Acts quoting the same passage Jesus used about hardened hearing, and attributes the speech to the Holy Spirit speaking through Isaiah — where Isaiah 6 says it was the Lord.
Two years under house arrest, preaching without hindrance, and then the book simply stops. No verdict, no execution, no resolution. The story is presented as still running.

1.ctx: Theophilus (‘friend of God’) was probably a real person of some standing, perhaps Luke’s patron, as in Luke 1:3.
1.mean: Luke’s first book told ‘all that Jesus began to do and to teach’. The word ‘began’ implies that Acts tells what Jesus continued to do, now through his Spirit and his people. After his suffering, Jesus ‘presented Himself to them with many convincing proofs that He was alive’ over forty days, teaching about the kingdom of God. He told them not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for ‘the gift the Father promised’: ‘John baptized with water, but in a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’
1.big: Acts continues the story of what the risen Jesus does through his Spirit and his people.

1.ctx: The disciples still expected the Messiah to restore Israel’s political independence.
1.mean: ‘Lord, will You at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?’ Jesus does not deny that God has plans for Israel, but redirects them: ‘It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by His own authority. But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.’ Instead of calculating dates, they are to be witnesses. Then ‘He was taken up, and a cloud hid Him from their sight.’ Two men in white say: ‘This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven.’
1.big: The risen Jesus ascends to heaven, sends his followers as witnesses to the world, and will return in the same way.
1.diff: Christians differ on whether God still has a distinct future for the nation of Israel (compare Romans 11:25–29). Many Reformed and Catholic interpreters see the promises fulfilled in Christ and the church of Jews and Gentiles; dispensationalists and others expect a future national restoration. Jesus’ answer here leaves the timing with the Father.

1.ctx: A ‘Sabbath day’s journey’ was 2,000 cubits, just over half a mile (BSB footnote), the distance Jewish tradition allowed on the Sabbath. The number twelve matched the twelve tribes of Israel.
1.mean: The eleven return to Jerusalem and devote themselves to prayer, ‘along with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with His brothers’, once sceptical (John 7:5), now believers. About a hundred and twenty gather. Peter explains that Scripture foretold Judas’s betrayal and his replacement (Psalms 69:25; 109:8). The new apostle must have been with them from John’s baptism to the ascension, to be ‘a witness with us of His resurrection’. They propose two men, pray, ‘Lord, You know everyone’s heart. Show us which of these two You have chosen’, and cast lots. The lot falls to Matthias.
1.big: The apostles are restored to twelve, chosen by prayer, to be witnesses of the resurrection.
1.diff: This is the last time lots are used in the Bible to discover God’s will. After Pentecost the church is guided by the Spirit, Scripture and prayerful discernment. Judas’s death is described differently here (falling headlong) and in Matthew 27:5 (hanging); many suggest both happened, with the body later falling, and that both accounts link the field to his blood money.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

2.ctx: Pentecost (‘fiftieth’) was the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, a harvest festival when Jews from across the world came to Jerusalem (BSB footnote).
2.mean: ‘Suddenly a sound like a mighty rushing wind came from heaven’, and ‘tongues like flames of fire’ came to rest on each of them. ‘And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit enabled them.’ Wind and fire recall God’s presence at Sinai and in the prophets. The crowd of Jews ‘from every nation under heaven’ is amazed: ‘each one heard them speaking his own language’, ‘declaring the wonders of God’. At Babel God divided humanity by language (Genesis 11); here the Spirit begins to reunite them in the praise of God. Some mock: ‘They are drunk on new wine!’
2.big: The promised Holy Spirit is poured out, and God’s wonders are declared in the languages of the nations.
2.diff: Tongues at Pentecost were real human languages the speakers had not learned; Wesley noted the miracle was ‘in the mouth of the speakers’, not just the ears of the hearers. Christians differ on whether speaking in tongues continues today. Pentecostals (such as the Assemblies of God) teach that baptism in the Spirit is ‘an experience distinct from and subsequent to the experience of the new birth’, and that ‘the initial physical evidence of the baptism in the Spirit is speaking in tongues’. Charismatics in many denominations welcome tongues today without making them a necessary sign. Cessationists, including many Reformed Christians, hold that the miraculous sign-gifts served to confirm the apostles’ message and ceased with them. All agree that every believer has the Spirit (Romans 8:9) and is to be continually filled with him (Ephesians 5:18).

2.ctx: The ‘third hour’ is about 9am. Peter, who had denied Jesus weeks before, now preaches publicly in Jerusalem.
2.mean: ‘These men are not drunk…It is only the third hour of the day! No, this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel’: ‘In the last days, God says, I will pour out My Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy’. The Spirit is no longer for a few prophets but for all God’s people, men and women, young and old, slave and free, and ‘everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.’ Then Peter proclaims Jesus: accredited by miracles; ‘delivered up by God’s set plan and foreknowledge, and you, by the hands of the lawless, put Him to death’; raised by God, because ‘it was impossible for death to keep Him in its grip’. David foresaw it in Psalm 16: God would not let his Holy One see decay. David’s tomb is still there; Jesus’ is empty. Exalted to God’s right hand, Jesus has poured out the Spirit. ‘Therefore let all Israel know with certainty that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ!’
2.big: Jesus, crucified by human hands according to God’s plan, has been raised and exalted as Lord and Christ, and has poured out the Spirit.
2.diff: Verse 23 holds God’s plan and human responsibility together in one sentence: Jesus was handed over by ‘God’s set plan and foreknowledge’, and his killers were guilty. Reformed theology draws from texts like this that God ordains all that happens without being the author of sin; Arminian theology stresses ‘foreknowledge’ and holds that God planned the cross knowing how free people would act. Both affirm the two truths Peter states. ‘Calling on the name of the Lord’ (Joel 2:32, where ‘Lord’ is the LORD) is applied to Jesus (compare Romans 10:9–13).

2.ctx: ‘Cut to the heart’: the crowd realises they share responsibility for rejecting the Messiah.
2.mean: ‘Brothers, what shall we do?’ Peter replies: ‘Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. This promise belongs to you and your children and to all who are far off—to all whom the Lord our God will call to Himself.’ Repentance is a change of mind and direction; baptism is the public sign of turning to Jesus; the promise is forgiveness and the Spirit. ‘Those who embraced his message were baptized, and about three thousand were added to the believers that day.’
2.big: The response to the gospel is repentance and baptism in Jesus’ name, with the promise of forgiveness and the Spirit.
2.diff: Baptism and forgiveness. Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran churches teach that God actually gives forgiveness and new birth through baptism; the Catholic Catechism says baptism ‘signifies and actually brings about’ the new birth (1215). Reformed Christians see baptism as God’s sign and seal of forgiveness received by faith: Calvin calls it ‘a sealing of those good things which we have by Christ’, adding that ‘forgiveness of sins is grounded in Christ alone’. Baptists and many evangelicals see it as the believer’s obedient public profession; they note that in Acts 10:44–48 the Spirit came before baptism. ‘You and your children’ (verse 39): Calvin and the Reformed tradition see here support for baptising the children of believers, as members of the covenant (Westminster Confession 28.4). Baptists read ‘children’ as descendants, and limit the promise to ‘all whom the Lord our God will call’, holding that only those who ‘actually profess repentance towards God’ and faith should be baptised (1689 Confession 29.2).

2.ctx: The first church met both in the temple courts and in homes.
2.mean: ‘They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer.’ Four marks of a healthy church: teaching, shared life, the Lord’s Supper (and shared meals), and prayer. Awe filled everyone. ‘All the believers were together and had everything in common. Selling their possessions and goods, they shared with anyone who was in need.’ They met daily, ate together ‘with gladness and sincerity of heart, praising God and enjoying the favor of all the people. And the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved.’
2.big: The first church was marked by teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, prayer, generosity and joy, and the Lord added to it daily.
2.diff: The sharing described was voluntary, not enforced common ownership: Peter tells Ananias the property was his to keep (5:4). It is a pattern of radical generosity rather than a political system. Whether ‘breaking of bread’ means the Lord’s Supper, ordinary shared meals, or both together, is discussed; in the early church they were often combined (compare 1 Corinthians 11:20–26).

3.ctx: The ‘ninth hour’ (3pm) was a time of prayer in the temple (compare 10:30).
3.mean: A man lame from birth, over forty years old (4:22), begs at the gate every day. He asks Peter and John for money. ‘Silver or gold I do not have, but what I have I give you: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!’ Peter takes his hand, ‘and at once the man’s feet and ankles were made strong.’ ‘He sprang to his feet and began to walk. Then he went with them into the temple courts, walking and leaping and praising God.’ Isaiah had promised that in the messianic age ‘the lame will leap like a deer’ (Isaiah 35:6).
3.big: In Jesus’ name a man lame from birth walks and praises God, a sign that the promised age has come.

3.ctx: A crowd gathers in the covered walkway along the temple courts (compare John 10:23).
3.mean: Peter disclaims any credit: it was not ‘by our own power or godliness’. The God of Abraham has glorified ‘His servant Jesus’, the one they rejected before Pilate. ‘You killed the Author of life, but God raised Him from the dead’. ‘It is Jesus’ name and the faith that comes through Him that has given him this complete healing’. Peter is gentle as well as direct: ‘I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your leaders.’ ‘Repent, then, and turn back, so that your sins may be wiped away, that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord’. Jesus remains in heaven ‘until the time comes for the restoration of all things’. He is the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15) and the offspring of Abraham through whom all the families of the earth will be blessed.
3.big: The healed man points to the risen Jesus, and Peter calls his hearers to turn to him for forgiveness and refreshing.
3.diff: ‘The Author of life’ (or Prince, Pioneer) is a striking title: the one they killed is the source of life itself.

4.h: Peter and John before the Sanhedrin
4.ctx: The Sadducees, the priestly party, denied the resurrection of the dead. Annas and Caiaphas (see the notes on John 11 and 18) are still in charge.
4.mean: The authorities are ‘greatly disturbed that they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection of the dead.’ Peter and John are jailed overnight, but the number of believing men grows to about five thousand. Before the council, asked by what power they did this, Peter, ‘filled with the Holy Spirit’, says it was by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, ‘whom you crucified but whom God raised from the dead’. He quotes Psalm 118: ‘the stone you builders rejected, which has become the cornerstone.’ ‘Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved.’
4.big: Salvation is found in Jesus alone, the rejected stone whom God has made the cornerstone.
4.diff: Verse 12 is often challenged today as narrow. Christians of every tradition have held it because Jesus alone died and rose for sinners. They differ on the fate of those who never hear: Catholic teaching holds that those who through no fault of their own do not know the gospel but sincerely seek God ‘may achieve eternal salvation’ through Christ (Catechism 847); many evangelicals hold that salvation comes through hearing and believing the gospel (Romans 10:14–17). All agree it is through Christ or not at all.

4.ctx: ‘Unschooled, ordinary men’ means without formal rabbinic training, not illiterate.
4.mean: The council is struck by ‘the boldness of Peter and John’, ‘unschooled, ordinary men’, and ‘took note that these men had been with Jesus.’ With the healed man standing there, ‘they had nothing to say’. They forbid them to speak in Jesus’ name. Peter and John reply: ‘Judge for yourselves whether it is right in God’s sight to listen to you rather than God. For we cannot stop speaking about what we have seen and heard.’
4.big: Ordinary people who have been with Jesus speak with boldness, and must obey God rather than human authorities who forbid the gospel.
4.diff: This passage and 5:29 are foundational for Christian teaching on the limits of obedience to authorities. Christians are to respect governing authorities (Romans 13:1–7) but must obey God when the two conflict.

4.ctx: The church’s first response to persecution is to pray.
4.mean: They pray to God as ‘Sovereign Lord’, Creator of all, and quote Psalm 2: the nations rage and the rulers gather ‘against the Lord and against His Anointed One’. That happened in Jerusalem when Herod and Pilate conspired against Jesus: ‘They carried out what Your hand and will had decided beforehand would happen.’ They do not ask for safety but for boldness: ‘enable Your servants to speak Your word with complete boldness’. The place is shaken, ‘and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God boldly.’
4.big: Facing threats, the church prays to the sovereign God, not for safety, but for boldness.
4.diff: Verse 28 is another text, like 2:23, holding together God’s sovereign plan and the real guilt of those who crucified Jesus.

4.ctx: Barnabas, introduced here, becomes a key figure in Acts 9–15.
4.mean: ‘The multitude of believers was one in heart and soul. No one claimed that any of his possessions was his own, but they shared everything they owned.’ ‘There were no needy ones among them’, fulfilling the ideal of Deuteronomy 15:4. Landowners sold property and brought the money to the apostles for distribution. One example is Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, nicknamed Barnabas, ‘Son of Encouragement’.
4.big: Unity of heart showed itself in generosity, so that no one among them was in need.

5.ctx: A dark contrast with Barnabas’s generosity at the end of chapter 4.
5.mean: Ananias and Sapphira sell property, keep part of the money, and present the rest as if it were all. Peter: ‘how is it that Satan has filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit…Did it not belong to you before it was sold? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal?…You have not lied to men, but to God!’ Ananias falls dead. Three hours later Sapphira tells the same lie and also dies. ‘And great fear came over the whole church’. The sin was not keeping money, which was their right, but pretending to a holiness they did not have.
5.big: God takes hypocrisy in his church seriously; lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God.
5.diff: Peter says they lied ‘to the Holy Spirit’ (verse 3) and then ‘to God’ (verse 4), one of the clearest indications in Scripture that the Holy Spirit is God. Many readers find the severity troubling. Most interpreters see it as a unique judgment at the founding of the church, like Achan’s at the start of the conquest (Joshua 7), showing the holiness of the community the Spirit indwells; it is not God’s normal way of dealing with sin in the church.

5.ctx: The church meets in Solomon’s Colonnade.
5.mean: ‘The apostles performed many signs and wonders among the people’. Outsiders respect them but are afraid to join casually, ‘Yet more and more believers were brought to the Lord—large numbers of both men and women.’ People bring the sick into the streets so that ‘at least Peter’s shadow might fall on some of them’, and crowds come from the towns around Jerusalem, ‘and all of them were healed.’
5.big: God confirms the apostles’ message with signs, and the church keeps growing.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

5.ctx: The high priest’s party were Sadducees.
5.mean: Jealous, the high priest and the Sadducees arrest the apostles. At night ‘an angel of the Lord opened the doors of the jail and brought them out’, telling them: ‘Go, stand in the temple courts and tell the people the full message of this new life.’ At daybreak they are teaching again. The council sends for them; the officers find the jail locked, guards at the doors, and no one inside.
5.big: No prison can stop the message of new life when God sends his messengers.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

5.ctx: The apostles are brought in, but gently, because the authorities fear the crowd.
5.mean: ‘We gave you strict orders not to teach in this name’. ‘But Peter and the other apostles replied, “We must obey God rather than men.”’ They repeat the gospel: ‘The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you had killed by hanging Him on a tree. God exalted Him to His right hand as Prince and Savior, in order to grant repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel. We are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey Him.’
5.big: The apostles obey God rather than men, and proclaim Jesus as the exalted Prince and Saviour.
5.diff: ‘God exalted Him…to grant repentance’ is one of several texts presenting repentance itself as God’s gift (compare 11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25). Reformed theology sees this as God’s effective work; Arminian theology as grace enabling a response people can still refuse. Both agree no one repents without God’s grace.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

5.ctx: Gamaliel was a leading Pharisee and teacher of the law, and Paul’s own teacher (22:3).
5.mean: The council wants to kill the apostles. Gamaliel urges caution, citing two failed movements: Theudas, and Judas the Galilean (see the drop-down). ‘if their purpose or endeavor is of human origin, it will fail. But if it is from God, you will not be able to stop them. You may even find yourselves fighting against God.’ They flog the apostles and let them go. ‘The apostles left the Sanhedrin, rejoicing that they had been counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name.’ ‘Every day, in the temple courts and from house to house, they did not stop teaching’.
5.big: The apostles rejoice to suffer for Jesus’ name and keep teaching, while even a cautious opponent admits they may be from God.
5.diff: Gamaliel’s principle, that what is of God will survive, proves true here, but it is not a reliable test in every case: many false movements have lasted a long time.

b: Gamaliel mentions two failed rebels: Theudas, with about four hundred men, and after him Judas the Galilean ‘in the days of the census’. Josephus also mentions both. He describes Judas as the man who led a revolt ‘when Cyrenius came to take an account of the estates of the Jews’, the census of AD 6. But Josephus’s Theudas, a self-styled prophet who promised to part the Jordan and was beheaded, appears under the governor Fadus, about AD 44–46. That is a decade after Gamaliel’s speech, and after Judas, not before.

Possible explanations. (1) Gamaliel’s Theudas was an earlier rebel, not the one Josephus describes; F. F. Bruce suggests he was probably one of the many who rose up in the disorders after Herod the Great’s death in 4 BC, which Josephus does not record in full. (2) Some scholars think Luke has made a mistake, perhaps through misreading Josephus; but that would require Acts to be written after AD 93, which most scholars think unlikely, and the details (four hundred men; no Jordan miracle) do not match well. (3) Josephus himself could be mistaken. No explanation is certain; the first is reasonable and widely held by those who think Luke reliable elsewhere.

6.ctx: ‘Grecian Jews’ (Hellenists) were Greek-speaking Jews, many from the Diaspora; ‘Hebraic Jews’ spoke Aramaic and were mostly from the land. Widows without family depended on charity.
6.mean: The Greek-speaking widows are being overlooked in the daily food distribution. The Twelve do not ignore it or take it over: ‘It is unacceptable for us to neglect the word of God in order to wait on tables.’ The church chooses seven men ‘full of the Spirit and wisdom’, and the apostles devote themselves ‘to prayer and to the ministry of the word’. The seven all have Greek names: those from the group that felt neglected are given the responsibility. The apostles pray and lay hands on them. ‘So the word of God continued to spread’, and even ‘a great number of priests became obedient to the faith.’
6.big: The church solves a fairness problem by sharing responsibility, keeping the word and prayer central.
6.diff: Many see here the origin of the office of deacon (compare Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:8–13), though the word itself is not used of the seven. The laying on of hands (verse 6) is seen by Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches as part of the origin of ordination; other churches see it as a commissioning with prayer.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

6.ctx: See the drop-down on the Synagogue of the Freedmen.
6.mean: Stephen, ‘full of grace and power’, does great signs. Members of the Synagogue of the Freedmen argue with him, ‘but they could not stand up to his wisdom or the Spirit by whom he spoke.’ So they stir up false witnesses: ‘This man never stops speaking against this holy place and against the law.’ They claim he said Jesus would destroy the temple and change the customs of Moses. The charges echo those against Jesus. ‘All who were sitting in the Sanhedrin looked intently at Stephen, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.’
6.big: Stephen, full of the Spirit, is falsely accused just as his Lord was.

hist.t: The Synagogue of the Freedmen and the Theodotus inscription (6:9)
b: Stephen’s opponents came from ‘the Synagogue of the Freedmen’, probably descendants of Jews taken to Rome as slaves and later freed, with Greek-speaking Jews from Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia and Asia.

In 1913–14 the archaeologist Raymond Weill found a 1st-century Greek inscription in the City of David naming Theodotus son of Vettenus, a priest and synagogue leader, as its builder, together with ritual baths and a guesthouse for travellers. It proves that Greek-speaking synagogues for Diaspora Jews existed in Jerusalem before AD 70. Because Vettenus is a Latin name, some scholars linked it with the Synagogue of the Freedmen; many others, including F. F. Bruce, think the evidence for that link is too thin.

7.h: Stephen’s Address: The Call of Abraham
7.ctx: The longest speech in Acts. Stephen answers the charge of speaking against ‘this holy place’ by retelling Israel’s history.
7.mean: ‘The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia’, far from the land and the temple. God promised the land to Abraham’s descendants but gave him ‘not even a foot of ground’, and told him his descendants would be enslaved four hundred years and then brought out to worship him. God gave him the covenant of circumcision.
7.big: God met Abraham far from the promised land; his presence has never been confined to one place.
7.diff: Stephen’s argument throughout is that God has never been confined to one place or building, and that Israel has repeatedly rejected the leaders God sent.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

7.mean: ‘Because the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph, they sold him as a slave into Egypt. But God was with him’ and made him ruler of Egypt. In famine, Jacob sent his sons to Egypt; on the second visit Joseph revealed himself. The family went down to Egypt, ‘seventy-five in all’. The pattern begins: God’s chosen deliverer is rejected by his brothers, yet becomes their saviour.
7.big: God was with Joseph in Egypt, and the brother they rejected became their saviour.
7.diff: Two details are often raised. (1) ‘Seventy-five’ (verse 14): the Hebrew text of Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5 says seventy, but the Greek Old Testament and a Dead Sea Scroll of Exodus say seventy-five (BSB footnotes there). Stephen follows the Greek text, which counts some later descendants of Joseph. (2) Verse 16 says the patriarchs were buried at Shechem ‘in the tomb that Abraham had bought from the sons of Hamor’, but Genesis says Jacob bought the plot at Shechem (Genesis 33:19; Joshua 24:32) and Abraham bought the cave at Machpelah (Genesis 23). Many think Stephen telescopes the two purchases into one summary, as speakers sometimes did; others see a slip in the speech, which Luke faithfully records.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

7.ctx: The time of slavery in Egypt.
7.mean: Jacob and the patriarchs died in Egypt and were buried at Shechem. As the time of God’s promise drew near, the people multiplied. ‘Then another king, who knew nothing of Joseph, arose over Egypt.’ He oppressed them and forced them to abandon their babies.
7.big: Even in oppression, God’s promise to Abraham was moving towards fulfilment.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

7.h: The Birth and Adoption of Moses
7.mean: Moses was born then, ‘beautiful in the sight of God’. Abandoned, he was adopted by Pharaoh’s daughter, and ‘educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and was powerful in speech and action.’
7.big: God prepared his deliverer in the very palace of the oppressor.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

7.h: The Rejection and Flight of Moses
7.mean: At forty, Moses defended an Israelite and killed an Egyptian. ‘He assumed his brothers would understand that God was using him to deliver them, but they did not.’ When he tried to reconcile two Israelites, one pushed him aside: ‘Who made you ruler and judge over us?’ Moses fled to Midian.
7.big: Israel rejected Moses, the deliverer God had sent.
7.diff: The parallel Stephen is drawing becomes clear: they rejected Joseph, then Moses, and now Jesus.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

7.mean: After forty years an angel appeared to Moses in the flames of a burning bush in the wilderness. The Lord spoke: ‘I am the God of your fathers’, and told him to take off his sandals, ‘for the place where you are standing is holy ground.’ Holy ground in the desert, far from any temple. The man Israel rejected, God sent back as ‘ruler and redeemer’. He led them out with wonders and signs, and spoke of a prophet God would raise up like him.
7.big: God made the desert holy ground and sent back as redeemer the man his people had rejected.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

7.mean: ‘But our fathers refused to obey him. Instead, they rejected him and in their hearts turned back to Egypt.’ They made the golden calf. So God gave them over to worship the stars, as Amos said: they carried the shrines of other gods, and God would send them into exile.
7.big: Israel’s history shows a repeated pattern of turning from God to idols.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

7.ctx: Stephen reaches the heart of the charge: the temple.
7.mean: Israel had the tabernacle in the wilderness, made to God’s pattern. David wanted to build a dwelling for God; Solomon built the house. ‘However, the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands.’ Isaiah 66:1: ‘Heaven is My throne and the earth is My footstool. What kind of house will you build for Me’? Then Stephen turns on his accusers: ‘You stiff-necked people with uncircumcised hearts and ears! You always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did.’ They killed the prophets who foretold ‘the Righteous One’, ‘and now you are His betrayers and murderers’.
7.big: God cannot be contained in a building, and those who claim to honour his house have resisted his Spirit and killed his Righteous One.
7.diff: Stephen does not say the temple was wrong, but that it was never meant to confine God, and that its time was passing now that the true temple, Jesus, had come (John 2:19–21).

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

7.ctx: Stoning was the penalty for blasphemy. Whether the council could legally carry it out under Roman rule is unclear; this may have been mob violence.
7.mean: The council is enraged. ‘But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked intently into heaven and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.’ ‘Look…I see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.’ They cover their ears, rush at him, drag him out and stone him. ‘Meanwhile the witnesses laid their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.’ Stephen prays, ‘Lord Jesus, receive my spirit’, and then, kneeling, ‘Lord, do not hold this sin against them.’ ‘And when he had said this, he fell asleep.’
7.big: The first Christian martyr dies seeing Jesus in glory and praying, as Jesus did, for his killers.
7.diff: Jesus is ‘standing’, not seated (compare Psalm 110:1), often taken as rising to welcome or vindicate his witness. Stephen’s two prayers echo Jesus’ words on the cross (Luke 23:34, 46), but addressed to Jesus himself, a powerful testimony to how the first Christians saw him. ‘Fell asleep’ is the New Testament’s gentle word for a believer’s death.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

8.ctx: The second stage of Acts 1:8 begins: Judea and Samaria.
8.mean: ‘And Saul was there, giving approval to Stephen’s death.’ A great persecution scatters the church through Judea and Samaria, all except the apostles. Saul ‘began to destroy the church. Going from house to house, he dragged off men and women and put them in prison.’ But the persecution only spreads the gospel further.
8.big: Persecution scatters the church, and the scattering spreads the gospel.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

8.ctx: Samaritans were despised by most Jews (see John 4). Philip was one of the seven (6:5), not the apostle.
8.mean: ‘Those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went.’ Philip proclaims Christ in a city of Samaria. People listen, see the signs; unclean spirits come out and the paralysed and lame are healed. ‘So there was great joy in that city.’ When they believe the good news of the kingdom and the name of Jesus Christ, ‘they were baptized, both men and women.’ Then the apostles send Peter and John, who pray for them ‘to receive the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit had not yet fallen upon any of them’. They lay hands on them, ‘and they received the Holy Spirit.’
8.big: The gospel crosses the old barrier into Samaria, and the apostles confirm that Samaritans belong to the same church.
8.diff: The Spirit received after baptism. The delay here is unusual in Acts. (1) Many interpreters, including Calvin, see a unique moment: God withheld the visible gifts until the apostles came, so that Samaritans and Jews would know they were one church, not rival ones. Calvin says Luke ‘speaketh not in this place of the common grace of the Spirit, whereby God doth regenerate us’, but of the special gifts of that time. (2) Pentecostals see a pattern: baptism in the Spirit as a second experience after conversion (compare 2:1). (3) Catholic teaching sees here the roots of the sacrament of confirmation, given by the laying on of hands (Catechism 1315 cites this passage); Calvin rejected this as making the rite ‘a continual law in the Church’.

8.ctx: Magic was widespread in the ancient world, and Simon had a large following.
8.mean: Simon had amazed Samaria with sorcery and was called ‘the divine power called the Great Power.’ ‘Even Simon himself believed and was baptized’, following Philip, amazed at the miracles. When he sees the Spirit given through the apostles’ hands, he offers money: ‘Give me this power as well’. Peter is blunt: ‘May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could buy the gift of God with money! You have no part or share in our ministry, because your heart is not right before God. Repent…’ Simon asks Peter to pray for him.
8.big: God’s gifts cannot be bought, and outward belief without a changed heart is dangerous.
8.diff: The word ‘simony’, the buying or selling of church office or spiritual things, comes from this episode. Whether Simon was truly converted is debated: he ‘believed and was baptized’, yet Peter says his heart is not right with God. Many see his faith as resting on wonders rather than on Christ.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

8.ctx: On ‘Candace’, see the drop-down. As a eunuch, the official may have been excluded from full participation in temple worship (Deuteronomy 23:1), though Isaiah 56:3–5 promised eunuchs a place among God’s people.
8.mean: An angel sends Philip to the desert road to Gaza. There he meets an Ethiopian eunuch, treasurer of the queen of the Ethiopians, returning from worship in Jerusalem and reading Isaiah aloud in his chariot. ‘Do you understand what you are reading?’ ‘How can I…unless someone guides me?’ He is reading Isaiah 53: ‘He was led like a sheep to the slaughter’. ‘Who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?’ ‘Then Philip began with this very Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus.’ When they come to water: ‘Look, here is water! What is there to prevent me from being baptized?’ Philip baptizes him, and he goes on his way rejoicing.
8.big: Isaiah 53 points to Jesus, and an African official becomes one of the first to carry the gospel towards the ends of the earth.
8.diff: The man was probably a God-fearing Gentile or a convert to Judaism. Verse 37, a confession of faith before baptism (‘I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God’), is not in the earliest manuscripts and is omitted from the BSB text (it appears in a footnote). It reflects early church practice.

b: ‘Candace’ was not a personal name but a title, used for the queen mothers who ruled the kingdom of Meroë in Upper Nubia (modern Sudan), south of Egypt, which Greeks and Romans called Ethiopia. Ancient writers including Strabo and Pliny the Elder mention these queens. The official in Acts was the treasurer of a real and powerful African kingdom, and his conversion marks the gospel’s first step towards ‘the ends of the earth’ (1:8).

9.ctx: Damascus had a large Jewish community. ‘The Way’ was an early name for the Christian movement.
9.mean: Saul, ‘still breathing out murderous threats against the disciples of the Lord’, gets letters to arrest believers in Damascus. Near the city, ‘suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice say to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?”’ ‘Who are You, Lord?’ ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting’. To persecute the church is to persecute Jesus himself. Saul gets up blind, is led into Damascus, and for three days neither eats nor drinks.
9.big: The risen Jesus confronts his fiercest persecutor, who discovers that to attack the church is to attack Christ.
9.diff: Paul tells this story again in 22:6–16 and 26:12–18, with small differences; here his companions ‘heard the voice but did not see anyone’, while in 22:9 they ‘could not understand the voice’ (the Greek can mean hear a sound without understanding words). Paul’s conversion is often presented as God’s sovereign intervention; Arminians agree that God took the initiative here, while noting that Paul could have been ‘disobedient to the heavenly vision’ (26:19).

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

9.mean: The Lord tells a disciple named Ananias to go to Saul. Ananias objects: this man has come to arrest believers. ‘Go!’ said the Lord. ‘This man is My chosen instrument to carry My name before the Gentiles and their kings, and before the people of Israel. I will show him how much he must suffer for My name.’ Ananias goes, lays hands on him, and calls him ‘Brother Saul’. ‘At that instant, something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes’. He is baptized, eats, and regains strength.
9.big: An ordinary believer obeys God at great personal risk and welcomes his former enemy as a brother.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

9.ctx: Galatians 1:17–18 says Paul also spent time in Arabia before returning to Damascus; Acts does not mention it.
9.mean: Saul ‘promptly began to proclaim Jesus in the synagogues, declaring, “He is the Son of God.”’ People are astonished: isn’t this the persecutor? But he grows stronger and confounds the Jews of Damascus ‘by proving that Jesus is the Christ.’
9.big: The persecutor becomes a preacher, proclaiming Jesus as the Son of God and the Christ.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

9.ctx: See the drop-down for Paul’s own account and King Aretas.
9.mean: ‘After many days had passed, the Jews conspired to kill him’, watching the gates day and night. ‘One night, however, his disciples took him and lowered him in a basket through a window in the wall.’ The hunter has become the hunted.
9.big: The former persecutor now suffers persecution for Jesus, as the Lord said he would.

b: Paul himself later describes this escape: ‘In Damascus, the governor under King Aretas secured the city of the Damascenes in order to arrest me. But I was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall’ (2 Corinthians 11:32–33). Aretas IV was king of the Nabataean Arabs (about 9 BC–AD 40), famous for Petra.

It is surprising that an Arab king’s official had power in Damascus, a Roman city. Historians note that no Roman coins are known from Damascus between AD 34 and 62, which may (or may not) mean Aretas controlled it for a time, perhaps granted by the emperor Gaius (AD 37–41). Acts says ‘the Jews’ plotted and watched the gates; Paul says Aretas’s governor guarded the city. Both can be true together. The episode helps date Paul’s early ministry to the later 30s AD.

9.ctx: Galatians 1:18–19 says this visit was three years after his conversion and that he saw only Peter and James.
9.mean: In Jerusalem the disciples are afraid of Saul, ‘not believing that he was a disciple.’ Barnabas, true to his name, brings him to the apostles and vouches for him. Saul speaks boldly and debates with the Greek-speaking Jews, the same group that opposed Stephen, and they try to kill him. The believers send him to Tarsus, his home city.
9.big: Barnabas’s encouragement opens the door for Saul to be accepted by the church he once persecuted.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

9.ctx: A summary of the church’s growth, then Peter’s ministry in the coastal plain.
9.mean: ‘Then the church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria experienced a time of peace. It grew in strength and numbers, living in the fear of the Lord and the encouragement of the Holy Spirit.’ At Lydda Peter finds Aeneas, paralysed for eight years: ‘Aeneas…Jesus Christ heals you! Get up and put away your mat.’ He gets up, and the whole region turns to the Lord.
9.big: The church grows in peace, and Jesus Christ continues to heal through his apostles.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

9.ctx: Joppa (modern Jaffa) was the port on the coast. ‘Tabitha’ (Aramaic) and ‘Dorcas’ (Greek) both mean gazelle.
9.mean: Tabitha, ‘always occupied with works of kindness and charity’, dies. The widows show Peter the clothes she made for them. Peter sends everyone out, kneels and prays, then says, ‘Tabitha, get up!’ She opens her eyes and sits up. Many in Joppa believe. Peter stays there with Simon, a tanner.
9.big: A life of practical kindness is honoured, and God raises Tabitha through Peter’s prayer.
9.diff: Peter’s words closely echo Jesus’ ‘Talitha koum’ (Mark 5:41). Staying with a tanner, whose work with dead animals made him ritually unclean in many Jews’ eyes, prepares for Peter’s vision in chapter 10.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 1 (chs. 1–13), CCEL

10.ctx: Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea. A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers. ‘God-fearing’ Gentiles worshipped Israel’s God without becoming full converts.
10.mean: Cornelius, a centurion, and his household are ‘devout and God-fearing’; he gives generously and prays regularly. At 3pm, the hour of prayer, an angel tells him: ‘Your prayers and gifts to the poor have ascended as a memorial offering before God.’ He is to send to Joppa for Simon Peter. Cornelius sends two servants and a devout soldier.
10.big: God hears a seeking Gentile and arranges for him to hear the gospel.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vols. 1–2, CCEL

10.ctx: Jewish food laws (Leviticus 11) separated Jews from Gentiles, since sharing a meal with Gentiles risked eating what was unclean.
10.mean: At noon on the rooftop, hungry, Peter falls into a trance. He sees a large sheet let down with all kinds of animals, clean and unclean. ‘Get up, Peter, kill and eat!’ ‘No, Lord!’ Peter answered. ‘I have never eaten anything impure or unclean.’ ‘Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.’ This happens three times.
10.big: God declares clean what he has made clean, preparing Peter for something greater than a change of diet.
10.diff: The vision is about people as much as food, as Peter explains in verse 28: ‘God has shown me that I should not call any man impure or unclean.’ It assumes Jesus’ teaching that declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19).

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vols. 1–2, CCEL

10.ctx: The timing is God’s: the messengers arrive as Peter is still puzzling over the vision.
10.mean: As Peter reflects, the Spirit tells him three men are looking for him: ‘Go downstairs and accompany them without hesitation, because I have sent them.’ They explain that Cornelius, ‘a righteous and God-fearing man’, was told by an angel to send for him. Peter invites the Gentile messengers in as guests, a first step across the barrier, and next day sets off with them and some believers from Joppa.
10.big: The Spirit leads Peter to welcome Gentiles under his roof.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vols. 1–2, CCEL

10.ctx: For a devout Jew to enter a Gentile’s home was a serious step.
10.mean: Cornelius has gathered relatives and close friends. He falls at Peter’s feet; Peter lifts him up: ‘Stand up…I am only a man myself.’ Peter explains: ‘You know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with a foreigner or visit him. But God has shown me that I should not call any man impure or unclean.’ Cornelius tells of his vision: ‘we are all here in the presence of God to listen to everything the Lord has instructed you to tell us.’
10.big: Peter crosses the barrier between Jew and Gentile because God has shown him that no person is unclean.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vols. 1–2, CCEL

10.ctx: Peter’s sermon is a summary of the gospel, much like the outline of Mark’s Gospel.
10.mean: ‘I now truly understand that God does not show favoritism, but welcomes those from every nation who fear Him and do what is right.’ Peter tells the story of Jesus, ‘who is Lord of all’: anointed with the Holy Spirit, ‘doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil’, put to death ‘by hanging Him on a tree’, raised on the third day and seen by chosen witnesses who ate and drank with him. He is ‘the One appointed by God to judge the living and the dead.’ ‘All the prophets testify about Him that everyone who believes in Him receives forgiveness of sins through His name.’
10.big: Jesus is Lord of all, and everyone of every nation who believes in him receives forgiveness.
10.diff: Verse 35 does not teach that sincere people of any religion are saved apart from Christ. Peter goes on to preach Christ to Cornelius as the one through whom forgiveness comes (verse 43), and 11:14 says the message was one ‘by which you and all your household will be saved’. Verse 35 means God welcomes people of every nation on the same terms; nationality is no barrier.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vols. 1–2, CCEL

10.h: The Gentiles Receive the Holy Spirit
10.mean: ‘While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard his message.’ The Jewish believers are amazed ‘that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on the Gentiles. For they heard them speaking in tongues and exalting God.’ Peter asks, ‘Can anyone withhold the water to baptize these people? They have received the Holy Spirit just as we have!’ They are baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.
10.big: God gives the Spirit to Gentiles exactly as to Jews, showing that they belong fully to his people.
10.diff: Here the Spirit comes before baptism, the reverse of 2:38 and 8:16. Most Protestants see this as evidence that baptism signifies a gift received by faith rather than causing it. Catholic and Orthodox Christians see it as an exceptional case in which God showed the Gentiles’ acceptance, with baptism still following as normal. Pentecostals point to tongues here, as at Pentecost, as the sign of Spirit baptism.

11.ctx: ‘The circumcised believers’ were Jewish Christians who held strictly to the law.
11.mean: Peter is criticised: ‘You visited uncircumcised men and ate with them.’ He tells the whole story in order. The clinching point: ‘the Holy Spirit fell upon them, just as He had fallen upon us at the beginning.’ ‘So if God gave them the same gift He gave us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to hinder the work of God?’ The critics fall silent and praise God: ‘So then, God has granted even the Gentiles repentance unto life.’
11.big: The Jerusalem church recognises that God has given repentance and life to the Gentiles too.

11.ctx: Syrian Antioch was one of the great cities of the Roman East, and became the base for Paul’s missions.
11.mean: Believers scattered after Stephen’s death speak only to Jews, ‘But some of them, men from Cyprus and Cyrene, went to Antioch and began speaking to the Greeks as well’. ‘The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number of people believed’. Jerusalem sends Barnabas, who ‘saw the grace of God’ and rejoiced. He fetches Saul from Tarsus, and they teach for a year. ‘The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch.’ When the prophet Agabus predicts a great famine, the disciples send relief to Judea ‘each according to his ability’.
11.big: Unnamed believers take the gospel to Gentiles, and a mixed church at Antioch is born, generous and well taught.
11.diff: ‘Christian’ was probably a nickname coined by outsiders, meaning ‘Christ’s people’. The relief sent to Jerusalem shows the unity between Jewish and Gentile churches from the start.

b: Agabus predicted ‘a great famine’ which ‘happened under Claudius’ (emperor AD 41–54). Josephus describes ‘a great famine’ in Judea under the governors Fadus and Tiberius Alexander, in the later 40s AD, when Queen Helena bought grain in Egypt at great expense and distributed it to those in need. The church at Antioch’s gift fits this setting.

12.ctx: ‘King Herod’ is Herod Agrippa I (BSB footnote), grandson of Herod the Great, king of Judea AD 41–44.
12.mean: Herod has James, the brother of John, ‘put to death with the sword.’ Seeing it pleases the people, he arrests Peter during the Feast of Unleavened Bread, guarded by four squads of soldiers, intending a public trial after Passover.
12.big: Persecution claims the first apostle’s life, and Peter is next.
12.diff: James is the first apostle to be martyred. Luke reports his death in a single verse and Peter’s rescue at length: God does not always deliver his people from death, and the church must trust him in both.

12.ctx: Mary’s house was a meeting place; her son John Mark later wrote the Gospel of Mark.
12.mean: ‘So Peter was kept in prison, but the church was fervently praying to God for him.’ The night before the trial, Peter sleeps between two soldiers, chained. An angel wakes him, the chains fall off, and he is led past the guards through the iron gate, ‘which opened for them by itself.’ Peter thinks he is dreaming until he is in the street. He goes to the house of Mary, where many are praying. The servant girl Rhoda recognises his voice and, overjoyed, runs to tell them without opening the gate. ‘You are out of your mind,’ they say. Peter keeps knocking.
12.big: God answers the church’s prayer in a way the church itself can hardly believe.
12.diff: Luke’s humour is evident: the praying church cannot believe their prayer has been answered, and leaves Peter knocking at the gate. ‘It must be his angel’ reflects a Jewish belief in guardian angels (compare Matthew 18:10).

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vols. 1–2, CCEL

12.ctx: Tyre and Sidon depended on Galilee for grain. See the drop-down for Josephus’s account.
12.mean: Herod, at odds with Tyre and Sidon, receives their delegation. ‘On the appointed day, Herod donned his royal robes, sat on his throne, and addressed the people. And they began to shout, “This is the voice of a god, not a man!” Immediately, because Herod did not give glory to God, an angel of the Lord struck him down, and he was eaten by worms and died. But the word of God continued to spread and multiply.’ The persecutor dies; the word he tried to stop goes on.
12.big: The king who claimed divine honours dies, while the word of God he opposed keeps spreading.

hist.t: The death of Herod Agrippa I (12:20–23)
b: The Jewish historian Josephus tells the same story independently. In AD 44, at games in Caesarea in honour of the emperor, Agrippa appeared in a robe ‘woven entirely of silver’ that blazed in the morning sun. Flatterers hailed him as a god, and he did not rebuke them. He was immediately seized by severe pains in his stomach and died after five days, aged 54. Josephus has him say, ‘I, whom you call a god’, am now commanded to die.

Luke and Josephus agree on the place, the royal robes, the people’s cry that he was a god, his failure to give God the glory, and the sudden painful illness. Luke sees the hand of God (‘an angel of the Lord struck him down’); Josephus sees Providence, with an owl as an omen. It is one of the clearest points where Acts can be checked against an outside source.

13.ctx: The leaders at Antioch were remarkably diverse: Barnabas from Cyprus, Simeon ‘Niger’ (‘black’), Lucius from North Africa, Manaen who grew up with Herod Antipas, and Saul from Tarsus.
13.mean: ‘While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.”’ After more fasting and prayer, they lay hands on them and send them off. Missions begin in a worshipping, praying church.
13.big: The Spirit calls and the church sends: mission is born in worship and prayer.
13.diff: The Spirit speaks in the first person (‘for Me…I have called them’), the language of a person, not a force.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vols. 1–2, CCEL

13.ctx: Cyprus was Barnabas’s home. Paphos was the seat of the Roman governor. See the drop-down on Sergius Paulus.
13.mean: They preach in the synagogues across Cyprus. At Paphos the proconsul Sergius Paulus, ‘a man of intelligence’, wants to hear the word of God, but a Jewish sorcerer called Bar-Jesus or Elymas tries to turn him away. ‘Then Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit’, rebukes him: ‘you will be blind and unable to see the light of the sun.’ Immediately darkness falls on him. ‘When the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed, for he was astonished at the teaching about the Lord.’
13.big: God’s word triumphs over opposition, and a Roman governor believes.
13.diff: ‘Saul, who was also called Paul’: he probably had both names from birth, Saul (Hebrew) among Jews and Paul (Latin, Paullus) as a Roman citizen. From here on Luke uses Paul, as he moves into the Gentile world.

b: Luke correctly calls Sergius Paulus a ‘proconsul’, the title of the governor of a senatorial province, which Cyprus was at the time. Inscriptions mention two or possibly three men called Sergius Paulus in the 1st century, and some scholars have linked one of them with Paul’s convert. None can be identified with him for certain.

13.ctx: Pisidian Antioch was a Roman colony in the interior of Asia Minor (not Syrian Antioch). Excavations there have uncovered a sanctuary of the emperor cult. Synagogue services included readings from the Law and the Prophets, after which visitors might be invited to speak.
13.mean: John Mark leaves them at Perga and returns to Jerusalem. At Antioch, invited to speak, Paul retells Israel’s history: God chose the fathers, brought them out of Egypt, gave them judges and kings, and raised up David. ‘From the descendants of this man, God has brought to Israel the Savior Jesus, as He promised.’ Jerusalem’s leaders condemned him, fulfilling the prophets, but God raised him from the dead, ‘never to see decay’. Then the heart of Paul’s gospel: ‘through Jesus the forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you. Through Him everyone who believes is justified from everything from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses.’
13.big: God’s promises to Israel are fulfilled in Jesus, through whom everyone who believes is forgiven and justified.
13.diff: Verse 39 is the only place in Acts where Paul speaks of justification, in words that match his letters (Galatians 2:16; Romans 3:28). John Mark’s departure later causes the split between Paul and Barnabas (15:37–39).

13.ctx: The next Sabbath, almost the whole city comes.
13.mean: Many Jews and converts follow Paul and Barnabas, who urge them ‘to continue in the grace of God.’ Next Sabbath the crowds come, and some Jewish leaders, jealous, contradict Paul. He and Barnabas reply: ‘It was necessary to speak the word of God to you first. But since you reject it and do not consider yourselves worthy of eternal life, we now turn to the Gentiles.’ They quote Isaiah 49:6: ‘I have made you a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth.’ ‘When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and all who were appointed for eternal life believed.’ Persecution drives the missionaries out, but ‘the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.’
13.big: The gospel goes first to the Jews, then to the Gentiles, and those appointed for eternal life believe.
13.diff: ‘All who were appointed for eternal life believed’ (verse 48) is one of the clearest statements in Acts linking faith and God’s choice. Reformed: God’s appointing comes first and faith follows; Calvin: ‘this place teacheth that faith dependeth upon God’s election.’ Arminian (Wesleyan): Wesley argued that Luke ‘does not say fore-ordained. He is not speaking of what was done from eternity, but of what was then done’: those who were then disposed, by God’s grace at work during the sermon, believed. Note too verse 46: the opponents ‘do not consider yourselves worthy of eternal life’, a real human refusal. See the key word Election.

14.ctx: Iconium (modern Konya) lay on the main road east.
14.mean: Again many Jews and Greeks believe, and again opponents stir up the city. Paul and Barnabas stay a long time, ‘speaking boldly for the Lord, who affirmed the message of His grace by enabling them to perform signs and wonders.’ The city divides. When a plot to stone them forms, they move on to Lystra and Derbe.
14.big: The Lord confirms the message of his grace, even amid division and danger.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vols. 1–2, CCEL

14.h: The Visit to Lystra and Derbe
14.ctx: Lystra was a Roman colony in a rural region where people still spoke the local Lycaonian language. See the drop-down.
14.mean: A man lame from birth listens to Paul; Paul sees ‘that he had faith to be healed’ and calls out, ‘Stand up on your feet!’ He jumps up and walks. The crowd shouts in Lycaonian, ‘The gods have come down to us in human form!’ They call Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, and the priest of Zeus brings bulls and wreaths to sacrifice. Paul and Barnabas tear their clothes: ‘We too are only men, human like you. We are bringing you good news that you should turn from these worthless things to the living God, who made heaven and earth and sea and everything in them.’ God ‘has not left Himself without testimony to His goodness: He gives you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons’. Then opponents from Antioch and Iconium arrive, turn the crowd, and stone Paul, leaving him for dead. The disciples gather round, and he gets up and goes back into the city.
14.big: Paul refuses worship and points pagans from idols to the living Creator, whose goodness is seen in every harvest.
14.diff: This is Paul’s first recorded sermon to a purely pagan audience. He starts not from Scripture but from God as Creator and Provider, an approach he develops at Athens (17:22–31).

b: The crowd at Lystra called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, ‘because he was the chief speaker’ (Hermes was the messenger of the gods). The Roman poet Ovid tells a legend set in this region of Phrygia, in which Zeus and Hermes visited the area in human form, were turned away by everyone except an old couple, Baucis and Philemon, and punished the rest. People who knew that story would be anxious not to miss the gods a second time. Inscriptions found near Lystra in 1909 mention priests of Zeus and a statue of Hermes dedicated to Zeus, which shows the two gods were worshipped together in the area. The site of Lystra itself has not been excavated.

14.ctx: Derbe was the furthest point of the journey. Rather than taking the short route home, they went back through the cities where they had been attacked.
14.mean: After Derbe they return through Lystra, Iconium and Antioch, ‘strengthening the souls of the disciples and encouraging them to continue in the faith. “We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God,” they said.’ ‘Paul and Barnabas appointed elders for them in each church, praying and fasting as they entrusted them to the Lord’. Back in Syrian Antioch they report ‘how He had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles.’
14.big: New believers are strengthened, warned of hardship, given leaders, and entrusted to the Lord.
14.diff: Paul offers no easy gospel: hardship is presented as the road into the kingdom. Appointing ‘elders’ in each church is an early pattern of local leadership; churches today organise this in different ways (see the note on 20:17).

15.ctx: The issue that also lies behind Galatians: must Gentile believers become Jews to be saved?
15.mean: Teachers from Judea tell the Gentile believers in Antioch: ‘Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.’ After sharp debate, Paul and Barnabas are sent to Jerusalem to consult the apostles and elders. On the way, they report the conversion of the Gentiles, ‘bringing great joy to all the brothers.’
15.big: The church faces its first great doctrinal crisis: is anything to be added to faith in Christ?

15.ctx: Usually dated about AD 49. How it relates to Paul’s visits to Jerusalem in Galatians 1–2 is discussed; see the notes on Galatians.
15.mean: Some believers who were Pharisees insist: ‘The Gentiles must be circumcised and required to obey the law of Moses.’ After much discussion, Peter speaks. God gave the Gentiles the Holy Spirit ‘just as He did to us. He made no distinction between us and them, for He cleansed their hearts by faith.’ Why put on them ‘a yoke that neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear? On the contrary, we believe it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.’ Barnabas and Paul tell of God’s signs among the Gentiles. Then James quotes Amos 9:11–12: God will rebuild David’s fallen tent ‘so that the remnant of men may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by My name’. His judgment: ‘we should not cause trouble for the Gentiles who are turning to God’, but ask them to abstain from food polluted by idols, sexual immorality, the meat of strangled animals, and blood.
15.big: Jews and Gentiles alike are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, not by keeping the law of Moses.
15.diff: The four requests are usually understood as practical concessions so that Jewish and Gentile believers could share fellowship and meals, plus a clear moral command (sexual immorality). Some see them as based on the laws for foreigners living in Israel (Leviticus 17–18). Church councils. Many traditions see this as a model for how the church settles disputes. Catholic and Orthodox Christians see in it the authority of councils of bishops. The Westminster Confession holds that councils may ‘ministerially’ determine controversies, but that since the apostles’ time ‘All synods or councils…may err; and many have erred’ (31.2–3), so they are tested by Scripture.

15.h: The Letter to the Gentile Believers
15.ctx: Silas, chosen here, becomes Paul’s companion on his next journey.
15.mean: The apostles and elders, ‘with the whole church’, send Judas Barsabbas and Silas with a letter. It distances Jerusalem from the troublemakers, who went out ‘without our authorization’, and commends Barnabas and Paul, ‘men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.’ ‘It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us not to burden you with anything beyond these essential requirements’.
15.big: The church’s decision, made with the Holy Spirit, frees Gentiles from the burden of the law.
15.diff: ‘It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us’ describes a decision shared with a person, not a force, and a church that sought the Spirit’s mind together.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vols. 1–2, CCEL

15.mean: The letter is read in Antioch, and ‘they rejoiced at its encouraging message.’ Judas and Silas ‘said much to encourage and strengthen the brothers.’ Paul and Barnabas stay, ‘teaching and preaching the word of the Lord.’
15.big: The gospel of grace, clearly defended, brings joy and strength to the church.
15.diff: Verse 34 (‘Silas, however, decided to remain there’) is not in the earliest manuscripts and is omitted from the BSB text (footnote).

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vols. 1–2, CCEL

15.mean: Paul proposes revisiting the churches. Barnabas wants to take John Mark; Paul refuses, because Mark had deserted them in Pamphylia. ‘Their disagreement was so sharp that they parted company.’ Barnabas takes Mark to Cyprus; Paul chooses Silas and goes through Syria and Cilicia, ‘strengthening the churches.’
15.big: Even godly leaders can disagree sharply, yet God uses the split to double the mission.
15.diff: Luke reports the conflict without taking sides. Mark is later valued by Paul (Colossians 4:10; 2 Timothy 4:11: ‘he is useful to me’), so the breach was healed.

16.ctx: Timothy’s mother Eunice and grandmother Lois were believers (2 Timothy 1:5).
16.mean: At Lystra Paul finds Timothy, son of a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father, well spoken of by the believers. Paul wants him to come, ‘so he took him and circumcised him on account of the Jews in that area, for they all knew that his father was a Greek.’ They deliver the Jerusalem decisions to the churches, ‘So the churches were strengthened in the faith and grew daily in numbers.’
16.big: Paul brings Timothy into the mission, removing an unnecessary obstacle to reaching Jews.
16.diff: Paul circumcising Timothy can seem to contradict Galatians, where he refused to have Titus circumcised (Galatians 2:3). The difference: in Galatia circumcision was demanded as necessary for salvation; here it removes a barrier for mission among Jews, for a man of Jewish descent through his mother (compare 1 Corinthians 9:20).
