16.ctx: ‘Asia’ means the Roman province in western Asia Minor (BSB footnote). Troas was a port on the Aegean coast.
16.mean: The Holy Spirit prevents them from preaching in Asia, and ‘the Spirit of Jesus’ does not allow them into Bithynia. At Troas, Paul has a night vision: ‘a man of Macedonia standing and pleading with him, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.”’ ‘As soon as Paul had seen the vision, we got ready to leave for Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.’ The gospel crosses into Europe.
16.big: God closes some doors and opens others, guiding the gospel into Europe.
16.diff: The sudden ‘we’ in verse 10 is widely taken as evidence that Luke joined Paul here as an eyewitness. ‘The Spirit of Jesus’ (verse 7) shows the Spirit is equally the Spirit of the Father and of the Son.

16.ctx: There was apparently no synagogue in Philippi, so Jews and God-fearers met by the river. See the drop-down on Philippi and Lydia.
16.mean: On the Sabbath they find women gathered for prayer by the river. One is Lydia, ‘a dealer in purple cloth from the city of Thyatira, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message.’ She and her household are baptized, and she insists they stay at her house. The first church in Europe begins in a businesswoman’s home.
16.big: The Lord opens Lydia’s heart, and the first European church begins in her home.
16.diff: ‘The Lord opened her heart’ is often cited in Reformed discussions of God’s initiative in conversion. Arminians agree that God’s grace opened her heart, while holding that such grace can be resisted. Both agree she responded by believing and acting. On household baptism, see the note on 16:25.

b: Philippi became a Roman colony after the battles there in 42 BC and was resettled with Roman veterans; Octavian (Augustus) gave it the title found on its coins, Colonia Iulia Augusta Philippensis. Colonies were miniature Romes, proud of Roman law and citizenship, which explains the charge against Paul and Silas of promoting customs ‘unlawful for us Romans’ (16:21) and the magistrates’ alarm at having beaten Roman citizens without trial (16:37–38).
Lydia came from Thyatira, in the region of Lydia in Asia Minor, famous for its purple dye. She was head of her household and evidently a woman of means.

16.ctx: The slave girl had ‘a spirit of Python’, named after the serpent linked with Apollo’s oracle at Delphi (BSB footnote).
16.mean: A slave girl with a spirit of divination, who earns money for her owners by fortune-telling, follows them shouting, ‘These men are servants of the Most High God’. After many days Paul commands the spirit in Jesus’ name to come out, and it does. Her owners, seeing their income gone, drag Paul and Silas to the magistrates: ‘These men are Jews and are throwing our city into turmoil by promoting customs that are unlawful for us Romans’. They are stripped, beaten with rods and thrown into the inner cell with their feet in the stocks.
16.big: Setting one exploited girl free costs Paul and Silas a beating and prison, because her freedom threatened others’ profit.

16.ctx: A jailer whose prisoners escaped could face death himself.
16.mean: ‘About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them.’ An earthquake opens the doors and loosens every chain. The jailer is about to kill himself, but Paul shouts, ‘Do not harm yourself! We are all here!’ Trembling, the jailer asks, ‘Sirs, what must I do to be saved?’ ‘Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved, you and your household.’ They speak the word to everyone in his house. He washes their wounds, ‘and without delay, he and all his household were baptized.’ He feeds them, and the whole household rejoices ‘that they had come to believe in God.’
16.big: ‘Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved’: the simplest statement of the gospel, given to a desperate man at midnight.
16.diff: Household baptisms (here and in verse 15; compare 11:14; 18:8; 1 Corinthians 1:16). Paedobaptists (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Reformed and Methodist churches) see them as consistent with baptising the children of believers, as members of God’s covenant family; the Westminster Confession says ‘the infants of one, or both, believing parents, are to be baptized’ (28.4). Baptists note that here the word was spoken ‘to everyone in his house’ and the whole household ‘had come to believe’, and hold that only those who ‘actually profess repentance towards God, faith in, and obedience to, our Lord Jesus Christ’ should be baptised (1689 Confession 29.2). The text does not say whether there were young children in these households.

16.ctx: Roman law protected citizens from being beaten without trial.
16.mean: In the morning the magistrates order their release. Paul refuses to slip away quietly: ‘They beat us publicly without a trial and threw us into prison, even though we are Roman citizens. And now do they want to send us away secretly? Absolutely not! Let them come themselves and escort us out!’ The magistrates, alarmed, come and appease them, and ask them to leave. Paul and Silas first visit Lydia’s house to encourage the believers.
16.big: Paul uses his legal rights, not for revenge, but to protect the young church he leaves behind.
16.diff: Why Paul did not mention his citizenship before the beating is unclear; perhaps he had no chance in the uproar. His insistence now would make it harder for the authorities to mistreat the believers in Philippi.

17.ctx: Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia. See the drop-down on the ‘politarchs’. Paul’s letters to the Thessalonians were written soon after.
17.mean: On three Sabbaths Paul reasons from the Scriptures, ‘explaining and proving that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead. “This Jesus I am proclaiming to you is the Christ”’. Some Jews, many God-fearing Greeks and leading women believe. Jealous opponents gather a mob, raid Jason’s house, and drag him before the city officials: ‘These men who have turned the world upside down have now come here’. ‘They are all defying Caesar’s decrees, saying that there is another king, named Jesus!’ The officials take bond from Jason and release him.
17.big: The message that Jesus is the suffering and risen Christ turns the world upside down.
17.diff: The charge was dangerous and, in a sense, true: Christians do confess another King, though his kingdom is not a political rival (John 18:36).

b: Luke calls the city officials of Thessalonica politarchai (‘politarchs’). Because no other example of the word was known, scholars once treated it as Luke’s mistake. In 1898 E. D. Burton collected inscriptions showing it was indeed the title of city magistrates in Macedonia. By the end of the 20th century about seventy such inscriptions had been published, around 40 per cent of them from Thessalonica itself. It is a small but telling example of Luke getting local detail exactly right.

17.ctx: Berea was about fifty miles west of Thessalonica.
17.mean: ‘Now the Bereans were more noble-minded than the Thessalonians, for they received the message with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true.’ Eagerness and careful checking go together. ‘As a result, many of them believed’. 17.ctx: Athens, past its political prime, was still the intellectual capital of the Greek world. Epicureans held that the gods were distant and pleasure (tranquillity) the highest good; Stoics saw God as reason pervading the universe and valued virtue and self-control.
17.mean: Waiting in Athens, Paul is ‘deeply disturbed in his spirit to see that the city was full of idols.’ He reasons in the synagogue and daily in the marketplace. Epicurean and Stoic philosophers debate with him: ‘What is this babbler trying to say?’ Others say, ‘He seems to be advocating foreign gods’, because he preached ‘Jesus and the resurrection’. They bring him to the Areopagus to explain his new teaching.
17.big: Grieved by idolatry, Paul engages thoughtful unbelievers wherever they gather.

17.ctx: The Areopagus was the ancient council of Athens, with authority in matters of religion and morals. See the drop-down on the ‘unknown god’ and the poets.
17.mean: ‘Men of Athens, I see that in every way you are very religious.’ Paul starts with an altar ‘TO AN UNKNOWN GOD’: ‘what you worship as something unknown, I now proclaim to you.’ God made the world and everything in it; he ‘does not live in temples made by human hands’ and needs nothing, ‘because He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else.’ ‘From one man He made every nation of men’, determining their times and boundaries, so that they would seek him: ‘He is not far from each one of us.’ Paul quotes their own poets: ‘For in Him we live and move and have our being’; ‘We are His offspring’. So God is not like an image of gold or stone. ‘Although God overlooked the ignorance of earlier times, He now commands all people everywhere to repent. For He has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed. He has given proof of this to everyone by raising Him from the dead.’ At the mention of resurrection some mock, some want to hear more, and some believe, including Dionysius, a member of the council, and a woman named Damaris.
17.big: Paul starts where his hearers are, but leads them to the Creator, to repentance, and to the risen Judge.
17.diff: Paul adapts his starting point (creation, their poets) without softening his message (repentance, judgment, resurrection). Some have thought the speech a failure, pointing to 1 Corinthians 2:2; most see it as a model of engaging a non-biblical culture, and note that people did believe. Natural theology, how much people can know of God from creation, is discussed by Christians from this passage and Romans 1:19–20.

hist.t: ‘To an unknown god’ and the poets (17:23, 28)
b: No altar inscribed with exactly these words has been found in Athens. But the 2nd-century travel writer Pausanias says that in Athens there are ‘altars of gods called unknown’, and Philostratus mentions ‘altars of unknown divinities’ there. Similar dedications are known elsewhere, set up when worshippers were unsure which god to honour.

Paul quotes Greek poets to his audience. ‘In Him we live and move and have our being’ is probably from the Cretan poet Epimenides. ‘We are His offspring’ comes from the Phaenomena of Aratus, a poet from Cilicia, Paul’s home province: ‘For we are also his offspring’ (BSB footnotes). Paul uses words his hearers knew about Zeus to point to the true Creator.

18.ctx: Corinth was a rebuilt Roman colony, capital of the province of Achaia, a busy trading city with two ports and a reputation for immorality. See the drop-down on Gallio and Claudius.
18.mean: Paul meets Aquila and Priscilla, Jews recently expelled from Rome by Claudius, tentmakers like himself, and works with them. When Silas and Timothy arrive, he devotes himself fully to preaching that Jesus is the Christ. Opposed in the synagogue, he moves next door to the house of Titus Justus. Crispus, the synagogue leader, believes with his household, and many Corinthians believe and are baptized. The Lord speaks to Paul in a vision: ‘Do not be afraid; keep on speaking; do not be silent. For I am with you and no one will lay a hand on you, because I have many people in this city.’ Paul stays eighteen months.
18.big: In a tough city, the Lord encourages his discouraged servant: ‘I have many people in this city.’
18.diff: Verse 10 speaks of people not yet converted as already the Lord’s. Reformed interpreters see God’s election here, which encourages evangelism rather than replacing it; Arminians read it as God’s foreknowledge of those who would respond. Paul’s tentmaking is often cited for Christian workers who support themselves.

18.ctx: See the drop-down: Gallio’s time in office is fixed by an inscription.
18.mean: The Jewish leaders bring Paul before Gallio’s judgment seat: ‘This man is persuading the people to worship God in ways contrary to the law’. Before Paul can speak, Gallio dismisses the case: it is ‘a dispute about words and names and your own law, settle it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of such things.’ The crowd beats Sosthenes, the synagogue leader, but Gallio shows no concern.
18.big: A Roman governor’s refusal to judge gives the gospel legal breathing space.
18.diff: Gallio’s ruling in effect treated the Christian message as an internal Jewish matter, sharing the legal tolerance Rome gave Judaism. A Sosthenes later appears with Paul (1 Corinthians 1:1); it may be the same man, converted.

b: Gallio, brother of the philosopher Seneca, was proconsul of Achaia, governing from Corinth. An inscription at Delphi mentions Gallio as proconsul and allows his time in office to be dated to about AD 51–52 (some scholars say 52–53). This is one of the fixed points for dating Paul’s life: his eighteen months in Corinth overlapped Gallio’s arrival, around AD 50–52. The bēma, the raised judgment platform in Corinth’s forum where the hearing probably took place, can still be seen. Claudius’s expulsion of the Jews from Rome (18:2) is also mentioned by the Roman historian Suetonius.

18.ctx: Cenchrea was Corinth’s eastern port. A vow involving cutting the hair recalls the Nazirite vow (Numbers 6).
18.mean: Paul stays some time, then sails for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila, having his head shaved at Cenchrea to keep a vow. At Ephesus he reasons briefly in the synagogue, declining to stay: ‘I will come back to you if God is willing.’ He lands at Caesarea, greets the church in Jerusalem, and goes down to Antioch.
18.big: Paul plans and travels, always ‘if God is willing’.
18.diff: Priscilla is usually named before her husband, which many take to indicate her prominence in ministry. Paul’s vow shows he still kept Jewish customs voluntarily.

18.ctx: Alexandria in Egypt was a great centre of Jewish learning.
18.mean: Paul travels through Galatia and Phrygia, ‘strengthening all the disciples.’ Meanwhile Apollos, an eloquent Jew from Alexandria, ‘well versed in the Scriptures’, teaches accurately about Jesus in Ephesus, ‘though he knew only the baptism of John.’ Priscilla and Aquila take him aside ‘and explained to him the way of God more accurately.’ He goes on to Achaia, where ‘he was a great help to those who by grace had believed.’
18.big: A gifted teacher humbly receives fuller instruction from a couple who explain the way of God more accurately.
18.diff: Priscilla and Aquila instruct Apollos privately in their home. Christians discuss how this bears on women teaching; at least it shows a woman taking part in explaining the faith to a male teacher, in a private setting with her husband.

19.h: The Holy Spirit Received at Ephesus
19.ctx: These twelve men seem to have been followers of John the Baptist’s teaching, like Apollos before Priscilla and Aquila taught him.
19.mean: Paul asks some disciples at Ephesus, ‘Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you became believers?’ ‘No…we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.’ They had received John’s baptism. Paul explains that John pointed to Jesus. ‘On hearing this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus. And when Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied.’
19.big: Disciples who knew only John’s baptism come to faith in Jesus and receive the Spirit.
19.diff: Most interpreters see a transitional situation: these men had not yet heard the full gospel of Jesus. Paul’s question shows he expected every believer to have received the Spirit. Pentecostals see a further example of a distinct experience of the Spirit; Catholics see a parallel with confirmation through the laying on of hands.

19.ctx: Ephesus was the leading city of the province of Asia. Tyrannus was probably the owner or regular user of a lecture hall.
19.mean: Paul speaks boldly in the synagogue for three months. When some publicly malign ‘the Way’, he moves his disciples to the lecture hall of Tyrannus and teaches daily. ‘This continued for two years, so that everyone who lived in the province of Asia, Jews and Greeks alike, heard the word of the Lord.’ The churches of Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis probably began in this period (compare Colossians 1:7; 4:13).
19.big: Two years of patient daily teaching in one city spread the word through a whole province.

19.ctx: Ephesus was famous for magic (see the drop-down). Exorcists used powerful names as spells.
19.mean: ‘God did extraordinary miracles through the hands of Paul’. Some Jewish exorcists try using Jesus’ name like a spell: ‘I command you by Jesus, whom Paul proclaims.’ The spirit answers: ‘Jesus I know, and I know about Paul, but who are you?’ The possessed man overpowers them all. Fear comes on everyone, and the name of Jesus is honoured. Believers confess their practices, and those who practised magic burn their books publicly, worth fifty thousand drachmas. ‘So the word of the Lord powerfully continued to spread and prevail.’
19.big: Jesus’ name is not a magic formula; it belongs to those who belong to him, and his power breaks the hold of the occult.
19.diff: Fifty thousand drachmas was roughly fifty thousand days’ wages (BSB footnote), a striking measure of the converts’ costly break with their past. The handkerchiefs and aprons of verse 12 are described as ‘extraordinary’; they are not presented as a pattern for later practice.

19.ctx: See the drop-down on Artemis, the theatre, the Asiarchs and the city clerk.
19.mean: Paul resolves to go to Jerusalem and then Rome. Then Demetrius, a silversmith who makes silver shrines of Artemis, gathers the craftsmen: Paul ‘says that man-made gods are no gods at all’, threatening both their trade and the honour of the great goddess. The city erupts; the crowd rushes into the theatre dragging Paul’s companions. Paul wants to go in, but disciples and some friendly Asiarchs (provincial officials) beg him not to. For two hours the crowd shouts, ‘Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!’ Finally the city clerk calms them: these men have neither robbed temples nor blasphemed the goddess; ‘the courts are open and proconsuls are available’. ‘For we are in jeopardy of being charged with rioting for today’s events’. He dismisses the assembly.
19.big: When the gospel threatens idols and the money they make, there is uproar, but God protects his servants.

hist.t: Ephesus: Artemis, magic and the theatre (19:19–41)
b: Ephesus was famous for magic; a type of magical formula was known as ‘Ephesian letters’. Burning books worth fifty thousand drachmas (a drachma was about a day’s wage, BSB footnote) shows how costly the converts’ break with the past was.

The riot took place in the great theatre, which still stands and held about 25,000 people. The temple of Artemis was one of the seven wonders of the world, and Ephesus proudly called itself her ‘temple guardian’ (neokoros, 19:35), a title found in inscriptions. Luke’s officials fit exactly: the ‘Asiarchs’ (19:31; over a hundred are named in Ephesian inscriptions) were leading citizens of the province; the ‘city clerk’ (grammateus) was the chief civic official, responsible to the Romans for any illegal assembly, just as he warns the crowd (19:40). See also the history panel in Ephesians.

20.ctx: Paul was collecting a gift from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–27; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4). Romans was probably written during these three months in Greece.
20.mean: After the riot Paul encourages the disciples and travels through Macedonia to Greece, staying three months. A plot against him makes him go back overland through Macedonia. He is accompanied by men from many of the churches: Sopater, Aristarchus, Secundus, Gaius, Timothy, Tychicus and Trophimus, probably representatives carrying the collection.
20.big: Paul’s companions from many churches show that his mission had created a united family of believers.

20.ctx: The meeting was in an upper room lit by many oil lamps, which would have made the air hot and heavy.
20.mean: ‘On the first day of the week we came together to break bread.’ Paul, leaving next day, talks until midnight. Eutychus, sitting in the window, falls into a deep sleep and falls from the third storey. He is ‘picked up dead’. Paul goes down, embraces him: ‘Do not be alarmed!…He is still alive!’ Paul goes back upstairs, breaks bread, eats, and talks until daybreak. ‘And the people were greatly relieved to take the boy home alive.’
20.big: The church gathers on the first day of the week, and God restores a young man to life.
20.diff: The gathering ‘on the first day of the week…to break bread’ is early evidence of Sunday as the Christian day of worship and of the Lord’s Supper at its centre. Luke’s ‘picked up dead’ most naturally means he had died and was raised; some read Paul’s ‘He is still alive’ as meaning he had not actually died.

20.ctx: Miletus was a port about thirty miles south of Ephesus.
20.mean: Paul walks to Assos while the others sail, then joins the ship. He sails past Ephesus, ‘because he was in a hurry to reach Jerusalem, if possible, by the day of Pentecost.’
20.big: Paul presses on towards Jerusalem with a clear sense of purpose.

20.ctx: The only speech in Acts addressed to Christians, and the closest in style to Paul’s letters.
20.mean: Paul reminds the Ephesian elders how he lived among them: serving ‘with great humility and with tears’, teaching ‘publicly and from house to house’, ‘testifying to Jews and Greeks alike about repentance to God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.’ Now, ‘compelled by the Spirit’, he goes to Jerusalem, knowing only that chains await him. ‘But I consider my life of no value to me, if only I may finish my course and complete the ministry I have received from the Lord Jesus—the ministry of testifying to the good news of God’s grace.’ He has not held back ‘the whole will of God’. Then his charge: ‘Keep watch over yourselves and the entire flock of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers. Be shepherds of the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood.’ Wolves will come, even from among them. He commits them ‘to God and to the word of His grace’. He worked with his own hands, remembering Jesus’ words: ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’ They kneel, pray, weep and embrace him.
20.big: Leaders must guard themselves and shepherd God’s flock, bought at the price of Christ’s own blood, holding nothing back of God’s word.
20.diff: Elders and overseers. The same men are called ‘elders’ (verse 17) and ‘overseers’ (verse 28, Greek episkopoi, from which ‘bishop’ comes). Calvin concluded that in Scripture ‘bishops differ nothing from elders’. Presbyterian, Baptist and many other churches therefore have one main office of elder or pastor. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches distinguish bishops from presbyters (priests), holding that ‘the bishops have by divine institution taken the place of the apostles as pastors of the Church’ (Catechism 862); they see the distinction emerging in the generation after the apostles. ‘His own blood’ (verse 28): some manuscripts read ‘the church of the Lord’ (BSB footnote), and the phrase can be translated ‘with the blood of His own Son’. Read as ‘God…His own blood’, it is a striking statement that the one who died is God; Calvin saw here ‘the unity of person in Christ’, where ‘the property of the one nature is applied to the other’. ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive’ is a saying of Jesus not recorded in the Gospels.

21.ctx: The voyage goes along the coast of Asia Minor and across to Tyre.
21.mean: At Tyre the disciples, ‘Through the Spirit’, keep telling Paul not to go to Jerusalem. After a week they all, with wives and children, accompany him to the shore and kneel on the beach to pray.
21.big: Believers who had never met Paul before love him enough to plead with him and pray for him on the beach.
21.diff: How can the Spirit both compel Paul to go (20:22) and tell others he should not? Most interpreters say the Spirit revealed that suffering awaited him, and the believers drew their own conclusion that he should avoid it. See also 21:8.

21.ctx: Philip was one of the Seven (6:5) and had evangelised Samaria and the coast (chapter 8). Luke may have gathered much early information from him.
21.mean: In Caesarea they stay with Philip, who ‘had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.’ The prophet Agabus takes Paul’s belt, binds his own hands and feet: ‘The Holy Spirit says: “In this way the Jews of Jerusalem will bind the owner of this belt and hand him over to the Gentiles.”’ Everyone pleads with Paul not to go. ‘I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.’ ‘The Lord’s will be done.’
21.big: Paul goes to Jerusalem knowing the cost, and his friends entrust him to the Lord’s will.
21.diff: This passage distinguishes a genuine prophetic message (Paul will be bound) from the conclusion people drew from it (so he should not go). Philip’s prophesying daughters fulfil Joel’s promise (‘your sons and daughters will prophesy’, 2:17) and are part of the discussion of women’s ministry.

21.ctx: James the Lord’s brother leads the Jerusalem church. A Nazirite-type vow (Numbers 6) ended with sacrifices and shaving the head.
21.mean: James and the elders welcome Paul and praise God for the Gentiles. But many thousands of Jewish believers, ‘all of them are zealous for the law’, have heard that Paul teaches Jews abroad to abandon Moses and stop circumcising their children. They suggest he join four men completing a vow and pay their expenses, ‘Then everyone will know that there is no truth to these rumors about you, but that you also live in obedience to the law.’ They restate that Gentile believers were asked only to keep the four requirements. Paul agrees.
21.big: Paul accommodates Jewish believers’ scruples to show he has not abandoned his people or their law.
21.diff: Paul’s action here has been debated since the early church. Calvin judged he acted rightly, ‘not moved thereunto by his own conscience, but for their sakes’, and that he ‘did not dissemble’: it was permissible as long as it was not done as a religious duty, but ‘only to support the weak’. Others think it was a compromise that backfired. Compare 1 Corinthians 9:20: ‘To the Jews I became like a Jew, to win the Jews.’

21.ctx: Trophimus was a Gentile from Ephesus. Gentiles were forbidden, on pain of death, to pass the barrier into the temple’s inner courts (see the drop-down at Ephesians 2:11).
21.mean: Near the end of the seven days, Jews from Asia see Paul in the temple and stir up the crowd: ‘This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against our people and against our law and against this place. Furthermore, he has brought Greeks into the temple’. They had seen Trophimus with him in the city and assumed the worst. The city is in uproar; they drag Paul out of the temple and the gates are shut. They are trying to kill him when the Roman commander arrives with soldiers. He arrests Paul in chains, but the crowd is so violent the soldiers have to carry Paul up the steps to the barracks, the crowd shouting, ‘Away with him!’
21.big: A false rumour turns a crowd into a mob, and Paul is saved from death only by Roman soldiers.

21.ctx: The barracks were in the Antonia Fortress, overlooking the temple courts. See the drop-down on ‘the Egyptian’.
21.mean: At the barracks Paul asks in Greek to speak, surprising the commander, who took him for ‘the Egyptian’ rebel. ‘I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no ordinary city.’ Standing on the steps, he motions to the crowd and speaks to them in their own language (Hebrew or Aramaic). A great hush falls.
21.big: Even in chains, Paul seizes the chance to speak to the crowd that wanted him dead.

b: The Roman commander assumed Paul was ‘the Egyptian who incited a rebellion some time ago and led four thousand members of the “Assassins” into the wilderness’. Josephus also describes this man. About AD 54, under the governor Felix, an Egyptian claiming to be a prophet led a large crowd to the Mount of Olives, promising that Jerusalem’s walls would fall at his command. Felix’s troops scattered them with bloodshed, but the Egyptian escaped. The ‘Assassins’ (Greek sikarioi, from Latin sicarii, ‘dagger-men’) were militant Jewish nationalists of the time who carried concealed daggers to kill those they regarded as enemies of the nation.

22.ctx: Paul’s second telling of his conversion (compare 9:1–19; 26:9–18), shaped for a Jewish audience.
22.mean: Paul stresses his Jewish credentials: born in Tarsus, ‘raised in this city’, ‘educated at the feet of Gamaliel in strict conformity to the law of our fathers’, zealous for God, a persecutor of ‘this Way’. He tells of the light at noon, the voice, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting’, and Ananias, ‘a devout observer of the law’, who said: ‘Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name.’ Later, praying in the temple, the Lord told him to leave Jerusalem: ‘Go! I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’ At that word the crowd explodes: ‘Rid the earth of him! He is not fit to live!’
22.big: Paul’s life story shows that the risen Jesus turned a zealous persecutor into his witness to the Gentiles.
22.diff: ‘Be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name’ (verse 16) is read like 2:38: by some as baptism conveying cleansing, by others as baptism picturing the cleansing received by calling on Christ in faith.

22.ctx: Flogging with the scourge was a brutal way of extracting information. Roman citizens were legally protected from it without trial. Citizenship could be inherited, granted, or in practice bought.
22.mean: The commander orders Paul to be flogged and interrogated. As they strap him down, Paul asks the centurion, ‘Is it lawful for you to flog a Roman citizen without a trial?’ The commander comes: ‘I paid a high price for my citizenship.’ ‘But I was born a citizen,’ Paul replies. The interrogators step back; the commander is alarmed at having chained a Roman citizen. Next day he brings Paul before the Sanhedrin to discover the real charge.
22.big: Paul uses his legal rights wisely, and his citizenship protects him for the journey to Rome.

23.ctx: Ananias son of Nedebaeus was high priest about AD 47–58, notorious for greed. Sadducees denied the resurrection, angels and spirits; Pharisees affirmed them.
23.mean: Paul begins: ‘I have conducted myself before God in all good conscience to this day.’ The high priest Ananias orders him struck. Paul flares: ‘God will strike you, you whitewashed wall!’ Told he has insulted the high priest, he says, ‘I was not aware that he was the high priest’, and quotes Exodus 22:28. Then, seeing the council divided, he calls out: ‘I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee. It is because of my hope in the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.’ The Pharisees and Sadducees fall out, some Pharisees defend him, and the commander has to rescue him again. That night ‘the Lord stood near Paul and said, “Take courage! As you have testified about Me in Jerusalem, so also you must testify in Rome.”’
23.big: In the middle of conflict and danger, the Lord stands by Paul and promises he will testify in Rome.
23.diff: Why Paul did not recognise the high priest is unclear: poor eyesight, an informal meeting, or irony (‘I did not think a man acting like that could be the high priest’). Opinions differ on whether his appeal to the resurrection was shrewd or questionable; it was true, since the resurrection of Jesus was the heart of the dispute. Luke reports it without comment.

23.ctx: Oath-bound assassination plots were not unknown in this troubled period.
23.mean: More than forty men swear not to eat or drink until they have killed Paul, and ask the council to request another hearing so they can ambush him on the way. ‘But when the son of Paul’s sister heard about the plot, he went into the barracks and told Paul.’ Paul sends him to the commander, who listens and tells him to keep it quiet.
23.big: God protects Paul through an ordinary young man’s courage and a Roman officer’s care.
23.diff: This is the only mention of Paul’s family in Acts, and suggests relatives living in Jerusalem.

23.ctx: Caesarea was the Roman capital of Judea and the governor’s residence. Antipatris was about halfway there.
23.mean: The commander sends Paul by night to Caesarea under a heavy escort: two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen. His letter, from ‘Claudius Lysias, To His Excellency, Governor Felix’, states that Paul is a Roman citizen and that the charges concern Jewish law, with ‘no charge worthy of death or imprisonment.’ (He tactfully says he rescued Paul because he learned he was a citizen; in fact he found out later.) Felix agrees to hear the case and keeps Paul in Herod’s praetorium.
23.big: A Roman officer’s report declares Paul innocent of any capital crime.

24.ctx: Tertullus was a professional advocate. See the drop-down on Felix and the officials of chapters 24–26.
24.mean: The high priest Ananias comes with elders and the lawyer Tertullus. He opens with flattery of Felix: ‘Because of you, we have enjoyed a lasting peace’. Then the charges: Paul is ‘a pestilence, stirring up dissension among the Jews all over the world. He is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes, and he even tried to desecrate the temple’.
24.big: Paul is accused of being a troublemaker, a sect leader and a temple-defiler.
24.diff: The flattery was hollow: Felix’s rule was harsh and his time in office troubled. Verses 6b–8a (Lysias taking Paul by force) are not in the earliest manuscripts (BSB footnote).

hist.t: Felix, Drusilla, Festus, Agrippa and Bernice (chs. 24–26)
b: The officials Paul faced are all known from Roman and Jewish historians. Felix, governor about AD 52–59, was a freed slave whose brother Pallas was a favourite at court. The Roman historian Tacitus wrote that he ‘exercised the powers of a king with the disposition of a slave’; his rule was harsh and corrupt, which fits his hope for a bribe (24:26). His wife Drusilla was a daughter of Herod Agrippa I. Ananias, high priest about AD 47–58, was notorious for his greed and was killed by Jewish rebels in AD 66.

Porcius Festus succeeded Felix, probably in AD 59, and died in office about two years later; Josephus contrasts him favourably with his predecessor and successor. King Agrippa II, son of Agrippa I, ruled territories north and northeast of Palestine and from AD 48 to 66 had the right to appoint the Jewish high priests; Bernice was his sister. He later tried to prevent the Jewish war against Rome in AD 66. Luke presents each of them in a way consistent with what other sources say.

24.ctx: Felix had governed for several years, so knew the situation.
24.mean: Paul answers point by point. He came to Jerusalem only twelve days ago to worship; no one found him arguing or stirring up crowds; they cannot prove their charges. ‘I do confess to you, however, that I worship the God of our fathers according to the Way, which they call a sect. I believe everything that is laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, and I have the same hope in God that they themselves cherish, that there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked.’ He came ‘to bring alms to my people’ and was found ceremonially clean in the temple. The only charge they could bring is the resurrection.
24.big: Paul’s faith in Jesus is the fulfilment of Israel’s own Scriptures and hope of resurrection, not a betrayal of them.

24.ctx: Drusilla, born about AD 38, was the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I; Felix had persuaded her to leave her first husband, King Azizus of Emesa, and marry him.
24.mean: Felix, ‘well informed about the Way’, postpones the case and gives Paul some freedom. Later, with his wife Drusilla, he sends for Paul to hear about faith in Christ Jesus. ‘As Paul expounded on righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became frightened and said, “You may go for now. When I find the time, I will call for you.”’ He was also hoping for a bribe. ‘After two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And wishing to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.’
24.big: Felix is moved by the gospel but puts off a decision, and two years pass.
24.diff: Felix is the clearest biblical picture of someone interested in the gospel who will not act on it. ‘When I find the time’ is one of the most dangerous phrases in the Bible.

25.ctx: Festus arrived as governor, probably in AD 59.
25.mean: Three days after arriving, Festus goes to Jerusalem. The leaders ask him to transfer Paul to Jerusalem, planning an ambush. Festus refuses and hears the case in Caesarea. The accusers bring ‘many serious charges that they could not prove.’ Paul: ‘I have committed no offense against the law of the Jews or against the temple or against Caesar.’
25.big: Two years on, the charges against Paul are still unproven.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL
‘Felix’ and ‘Festus’ (E. M. B. Green & C. J. Hemer), New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed.

25.ctx: A Roman citizen could appeal to be tried by the emperor (at this time Nero, before his persecution of Christians began).
25.mean: Festus, ‘wishing to do the Jews a favor’, asks Paul if he will go to Jerusalem for trial. Paul refuses: ‘I am standing before the judgment seat of Caesar, where I ought to be tried. I have done nothing wrong to the Jews, as you yourself know very well. If, however, I am guilty of anything worthy of death, I do not refuse to die.…I appeal to Caesar!’ Festus confers and replies: ‘You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you will go!’
25.big: Paul’s appeal to Caesar, a legal right, becomes the means of fulfilling the Lord’s promise that he would testify in Rome.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL

25.ctx: Agrippa II was the last of the Herodian kings, with expert knowledge of Jewish affairs.
25.mean: King Agrippa and Bernice visit Festus, who lays out the case. The accusers did not bring the crimes he expected: ‘They only had some contentions with him regarding their own religion and a certain Jesus who had died, but whom Paul affirmed to be alive.’ Agrippa wants to hear Paul himself.
25.big: To a Roman governor, the whole dispute comes down to one question: is Jesus, who died, alive?
25.diff: Festus’s summary (‘a certain Jesus who had died, but whom Paul affirmed to be alive’) puts the heart of the matter more clearly than he knew.

25.ctx: A grand public hearing in Caesarea.
25.mean: Agrippa and Bernice enter ‘with great pomp’, with military commanders and leading citizens. Festus explains that he found Paul ‘had done nothing worthy of death’, but needs something definite to write to the emperor.
25.big: A prisoner in chains stands before the powerful, and the pomp of the room cannot hide that he is innocent.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL

26.ctx: The third account of Paul’s conversion in Acts, the fullest on his commission.
26.mean: Paul is glad to speak to Agrippa, who knows Jewish customs. He lived as a Pharisee, and is on trial for the hope of Israel: ‘Why would any of you consider it incredible that God raises the dead?’ He describes his fury against the believers, then the light on the road and the voice: ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’ (Like an ox kicking against a prodding stick, he was resisting the one driving him.) Jesus appointed him ‘as a servant and as a witness’, sending him to the Gentiles ‘to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Me.’ ‘So then, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision.’ He preached that people ‘should repent and turn to God, performing deeds worthy of their repentance.’ It is all what Moses and the prophets said: ‘that the Christ would suffer, and as the first to rise from the dead, would proclaim light to our people and to the Gentiles.’
26.big: Jesus sends Paul to open blind eyes, turning people from darkness to light and from Satan to God, for forgiveness through faith.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL

26.ctx: To a Roman like Festus, resurrection talk sounded absurd.
26.mean: Festus shouts: ‘You are insane, Paul! Your great learning is driving you to madness!’ Paul: ‘I am not insane…I am speaking words of truth and sobriety.’ These events were ‘not done in a corner.’ ‘King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do.’ Agrippa: ‘Can you persuade me in such a short time to become a Christian?’ Paul: ‘Short time or long…I wish to God that not only you but all who hear me this day may become what I am, except for these chains.’ Leaving, they agree: ‘This man has done nothing worthy of death or imprisonment.’ ‘This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.’
26.big: Paul’s deepest wish, even for his judges, is that they would become Christians.
26.diff: Agrippa’s reply may be sarcastic, or a half-serious deflection; the older translation ‘Almost thou persuadest me’ is less likely. Paul’s response, ‘except for these chains’, is among the most gracious lines in Acts. ‘Not done in a corner’: Christianity rests on public events that could be checked.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL

27.ctx: The ‘we’ narrative resumes: Luke is on board. See the drop-down on the voyage.
27.mean: Paul and other prisoners are handed to Julius, a centurion of the Imperial Regiment. Aristarchus from Thessalonica is with them. At Sidon, ‘Julius treated Paul with consideration, allowing him to visit his friends’. Against contrary winds they reach Myra, transfer to an Alexandrian grain ship bound for Italy, and struggle to Fair Havens on Crete. ‘By now much time had passed, and the voyage had already become dangerous because it was after the Fast.’
27.big: Paul begins the long journey to Rome, as a prisoner but treated with respect.

b: Luke’s account of the voyage is one of the most detailed descriptions of ancient seafaring to survive. F. F. Bruce called it ‘one of our most important documents on ancient seamanship’, and James Smith’s classic study The Voyage and Shipwreck of St Paul (1848) traced the route in detail. Luke notes the sailing season (‘after the Fast’, the Day of Atonement in the autumn, when sailing became dangerous; BSB footnote), the northeast gale (Euraquilo), the undergirding of the ship, the soundings, and the anchors dropped from the stern.

The traditional site of the shipwreck is St Paul’s Bay on Malta, northwest of Valletta, and many scholars accept it, though others have been proposed. On Malta, Luke calls the governor Publius ‘the chief official of the island’ (Greek prōtos, ‘first man’), a title found in inscriptions from Malta.

27.ctx: The Syrtis were dangerous sandbanks off the coast of North Africa (modern Libya).
27.mean: Paul warns against sailing on, but the centurion follows the pilot and the owner. A gentle south wind tempts them out, then ‘a cyclone called the Northeaster swept down across the island.’ The ship is driven helplessly. They undergird the hull, lower the sea anchor, throw cargo and tackle overboard. ‘When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days and the great storm continued to batter us, we abandoned all hope of being saved.’ Then Paul stands up: an angel of ‘the God to whom I belong and whom I serve’ told him, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And look, God has granted you the lives of all who sail with you.’ ‘So take courage, men, for I believe God that it will happen just as He told me.’
27.big: When everyone has given up hope, Paul’s trust in God’s word gives courage to all.
27.diff: Luke’s nautical detail matches what is known of ancient seafaring and is often cited as evidence that he was an eyewitness (see the drop-down).

27.ctx: ‘The Adriatic Sea’ then included the central Mediterranean south of Italy.
27.mean: On the fourteenth night, soundings show land is near. They drop four anchors and pray for daylight. The sailors try to escape in the lifeboat, but Paul tells the centurion, ‘Unless these men remain with the ship, you cannot be saved.’ The soldiers cut it loose. At dawn Paul urges everyone to eat; he takes bread, gives thanks to God before them all, breaks it and eats, and all are encouraged. There are 276 on board. They run for a beach, but the ship strikes a sandbar and breaks up. The soldiers plan to kill the prisoners, but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops them. ‘In this way everyone was brought safely to land.’
27.big: God keeps his promise, and every one of the 276 reaches land, as Paul said.
27.diff: God’s promise (verse 24) and the practical means (staying with the ship, verse 31) are held together, as often in Scripture: God’s sovereignty does not make human action pointless. Paul’s breaking of bread with thanksgiving before pagans was probably an ordinary meal, though Luke’s words echo the Lord’s Supper.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL

28.ctx: Malta lies south of Sicily. ‘Justice’ (Greek Dikē) was the Greek goddess of justice (BSB footnote). Publius’s title, ‘first man’, is attested in Maltese inscriptions (see the voyage drop-down at 27:1).
28.mean: The islanders show ‘extraordinary kindness’, lighting a fire in the rain and cold. As Paul puts sticks on the fire, a viper fastens on his hand. The islanders conclude he must be a murderer whom Justice has caught. He shakes it into the fire and suffers no harm; they change their minds and say he is a god. Publius, ‘the chief official of the island’, welcomes them; Paul prays for his father, sick with fever and dysentery, lays hands on him and heals him, and the rest of the sick on the island come and are cured.
28.big: Shipwrecked strangers receive kindness, and God brings healing to a whole island through his servant.
28.diff: This episode is sometimes used, with Mark 16:18, to justify deliberately handling snakes, which most Christians reject as testing God (Matthew 4:7). Paul did not seek out the snake.

28.ctx: The Appian Way led to Rome; the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns were stopping points about 43 and 35 miles from Rome (BSB footnotes). The ship’s figurehead was the ‘Twin Brothers’, Castor and Pollux, patrons of sailors (BSB footnote).
28.mean: After three months they sail on an Alexandrian ship, via Syracuse and Rhegium, to Puteoli, where they find believers and stay a week. ‘And so we came to Rome.’ Believers from Rome come out along the Appian Way to meet them. ‘When Paul saw them, he was encouraged and gave thanks to God.’
28.big: The gospel is already in Rome before Paul arrives, and the believers there welcome and encourage him.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL

28.ctx: Paul is under house arrest, chained to a soldier, but free to receive visitors. Philippians, Colossians, Ephesians and Philemon may have been written in this period.
28.mean: Paul calls the Jewish leaders in Rome: he has done nothing against his people; ‘It is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.’ They have heard nothing against him personally, but know the ‘sect’ is spoken against everywhere. On an appointed day many come, and ‘He expounded to them from morning to evening, testifying about the kingdom of God and persuading them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets.’ Some are convinced, others not. Paul quotes Isaiah 6: ‘You will be ever hearing but never understanding’, and says that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, ‘and they will listen!’ Acts ends: ‘Paul stayed there two full years in his own rented house, welcoming all who came to visit him. Boldly and freely he proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ.’
28.big: Acts ends with the gospel proclaimed boldly and freely at the heart of the empire, the story still open.
28.diff: Why does Acts end without telling us the outcome of Paul’s trial? Some think Luke wrote at that point (about AD 62); others that the open ending is deliberate: the gospel has reached Rome ‘unhindered’, and the story continues in the church. Paul attributes Isaiah’s words to the Holy Spirit (verse 25), where Isaiah 6 says the Lord spoke them, another sign that the Spirit is God. Verse 29 is not in the earliest manuscripts (BSB omits it).
